speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It has to do with the report of the proceedings of this house yesterday.

Privilege-Mr. Bracken
Yesterday Your Honour ruled out of order a bill to amend the Judges Act introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In giving your reasons Your Honour stated as follows, as reported in Hansard, page 1569:
I would draw to the attention of the hon. member the fact that I am under the impression that this bill is out of order, because it involves an expenditure of money. So I rule the bill out of order.
And a little later on Your Honour made the following comment:
As I have said, I believe that the bill as drafted deals with public expenditures, and therefore is out of order.
It is clear that Your Honour's reason for ruling the bill out of order was your impression that it involved an expenditure of public money. I have not seen the bill, so I have no opinion on that subject.
However, in Votes and Proceedings of yesterday, No. 37, which document I believe is the binding and authoritative record of this house, there appears the following statement:
Mr. Speaker ruled that the introduction of such a bill was out of order on the ground that alterations in the salaries fixed by the Judges Act and judges retirement annuities, even by way of reductions, cannot be moved in the house by a private member, but that they can only be proposed by a minister of the crown on the Governor General's recommendation to be considered in committee of the whole by resolution prior to the introduction of a bill.
Mr. Speaker, nowhere in Your Honour's words can be read or implied the reason that appears in Votes and Proceedings. The matter is of some importance, as it affects the rules of the house. I do not believe that Votes and Proceedings should ascribe ' to Your Honour words or reasons which you did not use in addressing this house and therefore create a precedent for the future. The reasons which Your Honour gave are not those recited in the Volei and Proceedings, and the reasons given in Votes and Proceedings are, I suggest with all deference, not well established. If allowed to pass without protest they might eventually lead to a precedent, which would make it impossible for a private, member to move in committee of supply for the reduction of an estimate.
I would respectfully ask Your Honour to take the matter into consideration and to communicate to the house, at a later date, your opinion on the matters I have raised.

speechtext:
At this point of the debate on army estimates, I wish to draw the attention of the house to certain facts and make a few suggestions in the light of two important events of recent years, events which, whether we desired them or not, made of Canada, not only a nation, but a nation occupying a most important strategical position among the other countries of the world.
The first of those two historic events occurred without conflict and without any shock. To begin with there was Canada's constitutional change from a crown colony to a sovereign and autonomous state. Then came the more and more preponderant part our country has played in international affairs. Finally, the last five years of war have made Canada a nation among other nations of the world, a nation which on the morroW will proudly confer the title of "Canadian citizen" on the peoples of this vast and rich country, a nation which will have its own flag and, I hope, its own national anthem.
If Canada is one of the smallest nations in respect of her population, she is-one of the largest in terms of her contribution to victory in the recent war, and precisely on account of her international status and her astonishing growth, she has contracted heavy obligations toward her own people as well as toward other countries of the world.
The second historic event seized the world with fright. The day the first atomic bomb burst with unbelievably destructive force on the Japanese city of Hiroshima a new world took shape before us, a world in which there is. no place for international isolationism; a world where human society, whether British, American, French, Chinese or Russian, is joined; a world where it will be necessary to find peace formulas more fruitful than those dictated by national or individual egoism. By reducing the city of Hiroshima to dust that day the atomic bomb made of a point north of Alberta a strategic position comparable with
Gibraltar, the Dardanelles or the Panama canal. In that area are located perhaps the richest deposits in the world of uranium pitchblende, the basic material used by science to fashion the most murderous and destructive war weapon the genius of man has ever invented. From a glance at the world map one realizes that these deposits lie much farther from eastern Canada, for instance, than from such other countries as United States and even Russia. This should give every one of us Canadians serious concern when we consider our wealth, the immense possibilities of our natural resources, and the unlimited potential power of this young nation of ours.
The time has come for us to realize, whether we be English or French speaking, that our rich country, due to the fundamental changes and scientific developments which have taken place in the world during the last five or six years, stands to-day as an open field almost beckoning an invitation to potential invaders. The importance of this blunt fact can never be over-emphasized. Therefore, because of Canada's strategic position in the world to-day; because of the vulnerability of her rich soil which stands as a target at the crossroads of modern warfare, and because of the unprecedented chaos in which the nations of the world find themselves to-day, Canadians soon will have to decide whether they should build and maintain a first class post-war military force to protect their territory and meet their obligations toward humanity, or whether they should leave this task to other friendly nations. The last alternative obviously would mean the eventual establishment in Canada of British or United States forces, if not international forces, commensurate -with our strategic importance and our wealth in uranium and natural resources.
This is the issue that will have to be faced sooner or later. Whatever we decide, we should break away from the past.. We should adopt a new mentality, the mentality of a nation which has reached maturity, a nation where isolationism in the future will never be able to find serious supporters, either in Quebec or elsewhere.
As far back as we can go in history there have always been wars. For thousands of years the world has survived only as the result of armistices. After every great war the world has lulled itself with wishful thinking that there would be no more wars, only to be brusquely awakened by the clatter of more and more destructive war machines. I am one of those who hold the strong belief that as war always came in the past, dangers of war

still lie ahead. We all believe that to a greater or less degree, otherwise we would not be debating the army estimates this afternoon. On October 11, in a statement issued by the Canadian press, General Crerar made the following declaration:
The time is long overdue when we Canadians should think mainly in terms of the next generation and not so importantly in terms of the next election.
Then he continued:
I plead for the abandonment of "wishful thinking" and a general realization on the part of all Canadians that for the future we must be able quickly to mobilize important and efficient armed forces if we are to do our share, not only in maintaining the civilization we have so far reached, but also in developing our social relationships, national and international, to a yet higher standard.
In the years preceding the last world war, Mr. Speaker, the entire democratic world was more or less Maginot-line minded. There is a danger to-day that we may become atomic-bomb minded. The atomic bomb is not an antidote to war; it would only make wars more destructive, more inhuman and more terrible. Thank God if the wisdom of democratic leaders can gear this world to permanent and enduring peace; but due to present imperialistic rivalries bluntly displayed by the failure of the recent five-power conference I am much more inclined to believe that, barring a miracle, to-day we stand much closer to a third world war than we stood to a second world war on armistice day,, 1918.
To be prepared for dangers which may come is of the utmost importance. (Canada had its experience with unpreparedness in the past. Lessons of history must signify something to our generation and to this parliament. Therefore, because Canada has now become an important nation, she needs a well-reorganized, well-equipped, well-trained and well-paid army. She needs a permanent army of which every Canadian can be proud; an army which should be made attractive to all young Canadians of whatever racial origin; a Canadian army which will be a sign of strength, not of weakness. Obviously all this will cost money, but it must not be forgotten that the price paid for the organization and maintenance of an army constitutes an insurance premium on a policy which all civilized and progressive nations of the world are called upon to pay for their own security as well as for the obligations contracted toward other friendly nations.
Now. as to the participation of French-Canadians in the Canadian army, I was indeed proud the other day to hear the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) pay an impressive tribute to the French-Canadian soldiers. The
fMr. Arsenault.]
hon. member recalled that it was at Passchen-daele in 1917 that he won the Victoria Cross while fighting with French-Canadians. Many of those who fought and died at Passchendaele were sons of Bonaventure constituency, which I represent in this chamber.
I was also much interested to hear the hon. member for Nanaimo give a striking description of the outstanding performance of the French-Canadian soldiers from Le Regiment de Hull stationed at Vernon and Courtenay, British Columbia in 1943, many hundreds of whom were also from Bonaventure county. The hon. member knows that French Canadians are not cowards, as they have been directly or indirectly described during the last few years for purposes of political expediency. The hon. member knows that French-speaking soldiers have always given proof of as much bravery on the battle-fields as have any other soldiers in the world. But those young men from Quebec are looking for leadership; you can lead them, but you cannot drive them Let us not claim equality of sacrifice from them if at the same time we are not'prepared to give them equality of opportunity. The other day questions were placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the answers to which showed that there were more absent without leave from the army in the province of Quebec than m any other part of Canada. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there are. Obviously there are; and I am surprised to see that there are not a greater number absent without leave to-day in Quebec considering the attitude of some politicians toward those young men in recent years, and the treatment given the young soldiers from Quebec in certain parts of this country during the last world war. '
I have here letters of protest signed by 133 French-Canadian soldiers stationed at Vernon, British Columbia, in 1944, describing to some extent the harsh treatment that those young men received who belonged to the N.R.M.A. personnel, under the Pacific command. Scores of protestations were sent to province of Quebec officials and newspapers by French-Canadian soldiers stationed at Vernon, Courtenay, and many other points in Canada during the last war. As a result the matter was brought up by provincial members in the Quebec legislature, and the Quebec city council repeatedly sought, under resolution moved by Alderman Joseph Matte, copies of which I have here, to have a royal commission set up to investigate the treatment of French-

Demobilization-Army
speaking soldiers. But the investigation was never granted. The defence minister of that time, Colonel Ralston, took the responsibility to refuse it repeatedly. French Canadians once more felt that they had been frustrated in the granting of most elementary rights.
A large number of these young men could not say two words in English, and were farmers' or fishermen's sons who in the first instance should never have been brought into the army. They had asked for farm leave, but their requests were always flatly, systematically and bluntly turned down by stupid officers, in spite of the right they had to be granted farm leaves. The first chance they had to go home, they went home and they stayed home. Who to-day should be surprised to find those unfortunate young men on the AWOL lists, considering that everything has been done to make them hate the Canadian army? Who should be scandalized when French-Canadian soldiers throughout the war were treated in this country as poor relatives, when they were not depicted as cowards, zombies or shirkers, and then to be offered on the very eve of Japanese surrender sermons on equality of sacrifice and conscription for Japan? Surely that is a discriminating situation.
Let us give the young men of Quebec equality of opportunity in a reorganized Canadian army, as free of stupid brass hats as possible, and no one will have to come along in Quebec and preach equality of sacrifice to them.
And yet to-day there are scores of young French Canadians who fought throughout the whole war with the R.C.A.F. who volunteered for service in the Pacific, and who are told that they must accept their discharge, despite their wish to stay in the permanent force. I also know numbers of brilliant French-speaking officers in the army who are desirous of following a military career, but they are flatly discarded by the brass hats. This is done in spite of this government's policy of establishing in Canada a military force in keeping with the importance of our country and of our obligations.
I know that the Minister of National Defence is doing some housecleaning at the present time. He certainly deserves the support of all parties in the house for his outstanding performance as an upright, courageous, effective, sincere and far-sighted Minister of National Defence.
And if the committee wants to hear more about French-speaking Canadians not having had equality of opportunity in the Canadian army, may I refer bon. members to the list of personnel at National Defence headquarters in Ottawa at the time Colonel Ralston was minister. The following is the list of personnel:
Principal Secretary:	Miss 0. J. Waters
Deputy Minister (C): Lt.-Col. G. S. Currie, Deputy Minister (D): Lt.-Col. H. Desrosiers, Assistant Deputy Minister: Mr. Jack Pembroke. Parliamentary Assistant to Minister: Mr. W. C. Macdonald. Military Secretary: Colonel H. A. Dyde. Judge Advocate-General:	Brigadier
R. J. Orde. Director of Public Relations: Colonel F. X. Jennings.
Of the nine members on the staff, only one, Lieut.-Col. Desrosiers, was French Canadian.
Of the seventeen members on the branch of the general staff, there was not one French Canadian.
Of the twenty-eight members of the branch of the AdjutanLGeneral, only two were French Canadians, namely the Vice-Adjutant General, Brigadier M. Noel and the Director of Records, Col. C. L. Laurin.
Of the ten members on the branch of the Quartermaster-general, there was not one French Canadian.
Of the seventeen members in the branch of the Master-General of the Ordnance, again there was not one French Canadian.
The grand total for national defence headquarters in Ottawa stands at three French Canadians out of a total of 72. Is that what can be termed a Canadian partnership? And the same discriminatory situation applied all the way down the list, as far down as that little Quebec farmer's son who did not speak English, and found himself lost, hundreds if not thousands of miles away from his home, where he was often requested to speak "white", or had to hunt for a translator to try to explain his wants, if not his grievances, to the officers-some intelligent and broadminded, and others very stupid and narrowminded, but who, whether intelligent or stupid, did not know his mentality and were not in a position to find out what his aptitudes were because they did not understand his language.
It is under such circumstances that a certain category of politician during these last years has thought it a very smart idea to try to climb to power by representing the young men of Quebec as being disloyal at a time when scores of French Canadians were merely the victims of a disgraceful system and others of a stupid, shameful and anti-Canadian boycott in the Canadian army. Their plea for

Demobilization-Army

equality of sacrifice, made in a way which was interpreted in Quebec and outside of Quebec as being directed against Quebec, did not carry them very far. They had been warned over and over again of the depth of the ditch into which they were heading, but instead of taking the advice of the man on the street, they listened to the sweet whisperings of the men of Bay street.
But they learned at their own expense that there was no anti-Quebec faction in this country or among the servicemen which amounted to anything worth while. They were also bluntly told by the electorate on the same day that no political party can ever dream of getting into power or being maintained in office in Canada without securing a fair support from the French-speaking population of this country and that, in order to win that support, one must deserve it.
If human means can achieve equality of sacrifice on earth, and I do not know of any gauge yet invented by man to measure it, it will be achieved in our country the day equality of opportunity is assured to all young Canadians; of whatever racial extraction, creed or language. Therefore I submit that we should undertake a complete reorganization of our militia system, getting rid of anything that tends to restrict the army to the time-worn system of other years and taking the necessary steps to give French Canadians equality of opportunity in the Canadian army. I urge that a French-Canadian college, similar to the Royal Military College at Kingston, be established in the province of Quebec. In order to create a better feeling and improve harmony and efficiency, I suggest that members of both the permanent and reserve forces be given their training in various provinces and that all officers having French-speaking Canadians under their command be bilingual.
This would help young men from all parts of Canada to understand the problems of each other. It would provide an excellent opportunity for an important section of our population to learn both official languages of this country. This in turn would lead to greater unity. We will need greater unity because no one dare say that Canada may' not be the battlefield in another world war. Until now we have always thought of raising armed forces to fight in other countries in wars that at times appeared to be the business of others rather than our own. We know that our forces overseas helped to keep war away from this continent, but in the next war it is quite

possible that this fair land of ours will be one of the first to be attacked, not because of any particular animosity toward our people but because of the riches of our uranium deposits, our industrial possibilities, and the wealth of our resources. I think our returning veterans will agree that if another war should come, Canada will not go unscathed.
Speaking of veterans, and this is my last word, I would urge that we do all possible to help them rehabilitate themselves and that we see that they do not suffer as a result of their absence on the most unselfish job man ever took, that of offering his life for the happiness of others. If we treat our veterans rightly, they will be the leaders in the spreading of unity throughout the country. Then with our own national flag, our own national anthem and a truly Canadian mentality, w:e will be able to march shoulder to shoulder to that place in international affairs that belongs rightly to a young, virile and ambitious nation such as ours.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard a very strong plea for the consideration of one phase of national unity. I think this is one to which the minister probably will reply or in respect to which he will at least make some comment. Since the question of discrimination has been raised I am taking this opportunitj'' of bringing the attention of this committee to another form of discrimination, that is, discrimination in our army because of the unpopularity of a young man's political views. We like to think of Canada's army as a citizens' army, an army in which every young man, regardless of his political views, will have exactly the same opportunity and be given the same sort of square deal.
I regard it as unfortunate that during this war we did not follow the example set by the army of Great Britain. They encouraged every sort of discussion, including mock parliaments, in the British army, and a man was not penalized because he discussed current affairs from any point of view. We all remember the story of the eighth army in north Africa when a mock parliament was established at Cairo and the outcry there was when it was proposed to discontinue that type of discussion. I have good reason to believe that in our army, men who held views that were not alw'ays acceptable or in conformity with the status quo were sometimes penalized. In order to make myself clear I am going to cite one particular case of which I have intimate knowledge.
I am thinking of a young man who was a student at Queen's university. When he became of age he enlisted as a private in this

Demobilization-Army
city. He trained first of all with the armoured corps at Camp Borden. He was recommended for training as an officer at Gordon Head, British Columbia. He graduated from there as a second lieutenant. He was then returned to Camp Borden to qualify as a first lieutenant and was there for five months. At the end of the five months the young man was reported as having failed to qualify for the full lieutenancy and was struck off strength and sent to the Ottawa depot for disposal. At Ottawa he appeared before Brigadier Armstrong and was informed that he was released from the army, to be subject to recall under the mobilization act. The reason given was that he was incompetent as an officer. Now by chance this young man's father had an apartment to let, the mother having died. It was advertised, and one of the gentlemen who came to see if the apartment was suitable was a brigadier from national defence headquarters-I may as well be specific; it was Brigadier Nash. Knowing the father, he drew the boy's file, and he told the lad's father that this young man was reported to have extremely radical tendencies, that it was alleged he had incited troops to disorder, was incompetent as an officer, and had failed to pass the required examinations at Camp Borden. Now the only possible explanation was that this young man, who is known to me as a very quiet lad.-one who never took any particular interest in politics although his father was a former member of parliament-on one occasion, when there was a discussion group, joined in a discussion on the employment prospects which were likely to be found following the war; and it was undoubtedly on the basis of what happened on that occasion that this young man was let out or about to be let out of the army, to be recalled under the mobilization act. Fortunately the brigadier to whom I have just referred knew this boy's background and decided to give him another chance. He was transferred to the infantry camp at Aldershot, Nova Scotia. Before he went he was advised by national defence headquarters to ibe inconspicuous in his behaviour and to be generally pretty quiet, with the result that he failed to qualify at Aldershot, and when he inquired the reason, the reason he was given was that he was too quiet and had not enough initiative. He presented his case to the commanding officer at Aldershot, who overruled the recommendation that had been made to him, and the young man qualified as a lieutenant, against the reports which were made concerning him that he was not suitable officer material and so on.
In 1944 this young man proceeded overseas and took a commission in the British army. He served in all the major campaigns against Germany as a combat officer in the 21st army 47696-1041
group sector, and he was slightly wounded on D-day. When he recovered he volunteered for the airborne troops. He was at Arnhem. One of the war records photographs of the imperial army shows this young man with his rifle, and under it is the explanation that he was the last man to defend the headquarters at Arnhem. He attempted to escape from the Germans, and was captured when crossing a river. He was placed on a train, and with other persons he escaped from the train. He joined the Dutch underground1, and after several weeks of operations with the Dutch underground he succeeded in regaining the British lines; and then, because of his initiative and ability he was asked if 'he would work in Intelligence No. 9. I am quite sure that some of the military men here know the implication-of "Intelligence No. 9': as a matter of fact, highly dangerous work, highly secret work, operating week in and week out with the underground movement except for the times when they came out from behind the enemy lines; and for the remainder of the war this young man was constantly doing intelligence work behind the German lines.
I have seen his pass, which he brought back [DOT] with him, signed personally by General Eisenhower. It gives this young man the right to pass at any time through the allied lines without question, to requisition at any time any facilities he might require, whether it were a jeep, an automobile, or a plane, and that if he were accompanied, as the pass indicates, by persons in civilian clothes they were to pass through, if he vouched for them, without any further question. This young man was subsequently promoted to captain and-incidentally-awarded the Military Cross. While I am not advertising the book, he was requested by Macmillans Limited, a large publishing firm in Great Britain, who knew his story, to write the story, which is about to be published under the title of "Escape from Arnhem." Now, when he got back to the Canadian army, again he was reduced in rank to that of lieutenant, this being the rank he was given upon his return to Canada. The minister and his predecessor tell me, of course, that that is quite the normal procedure, that there is no authority to confirm that rank; and I am not complaining about that now. All I am doing this afternoon is to point out that here we have a young Canadian who has rendered very distinguished services to the country in this war;, he had initiative; he had everything that went to make a good officer, but because he was alleged to have extremely radical tendencies-
C.C.F.?

Yes, C.C.F.
Demobilization-Army
Why did they not send him to China?
He was let out of the army; and I have been toldi on the highest authority-I will use just that term-that this is not the only case of that type.
They should have sent him to the Chinese embassy.

I know the reference. I suppose some of my hon. friends are annoyed because a man of outstanding ability in this country, one of the few men born and educated in China, and who can speak the Chinese language fluently, Squadron Leader Chester Homing has been given a position by the government to go to Chungking, in spite of the fact that he is a C.C.F. supporter.
We are not annoyed.
Any man who happens to be a member of this organization has to have pretty high qualifications to get a position of that kind.
He would not be a member if he had the highest qualifications.

We will let that be a matter of opinion. But the proof of the pudding is in the eating.
I am bringing this story to the attention of the committee because I feel this way about it: if we are to have a people's army fighting a people's cause, if we are to have a citizens' army, we must see to it (a) that the army is under the control of the representatives of the people-in other words, that is answerable to this House of Commons; for we cannot afford to establish any armed force which is not under the control of this parliament; and (b) that in this army men have the right to express themselves, the right to discuss questions as other citizens have the right to discuss them, because they have to come back and live among their fellow citizens after the wars are over. We hope there will never be another war. But in order that they may exercise the rights and duties of Canadian citizens they should not merely be permitted but be given every facility to know the problems of their own country, to discuss those problems intelligently, and, like all others, to come to an intelligent conclusion.
I thought it best to discuss this matter not in a general way but by placing before the committee a case, every sentence of which can be authenticated from the records. I do not need to put the name on record; I will give it to the minister privately. That may be the way to deal with it. But instead of chewing over matters of past policy, I suggest that we try to formulate in our department of
[Mr. Coldweil.l
defence a policy that is consonant with the ideals of most of the young men and women who fought for this country in the last war; and to my mind that can be done only by building up an army that is a citizen's army in which men and, as far as there are women in the army, women as well, are free to think and to discuss the problems of the day and of their own country.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I wish to make only a brief comment on the remarks which have just been made by the member for Rosetown-Biggar. I followed with a great deal of interest his statement of the case of a particular officer whom he had in mind, and I am sure he knows I agree with him, as I believe every hon.. member agrees, that political opinions should not be made the basis for discrimination in any Canadian army. Any cases that come to my attention, and I have no doubt that any that came to the attention of any of my predecessors, were promptly and fully investigated. But I suppose we have to realize that in an army of two, three or four hundred thousand men, with a very large number of officers, and human nature being what it is, there will be some officers who do not adhere as strictly as they should to the principles which we here think should be followed. So far as all of us here are concerned, however, so far as I am concerned, no question of promotibn or advancement shall be affected by means of political opinions.
As to the right to express political opinions in the army, I agree so far as citizen soldiers are concerned. I am not quite so sure about the relatively small professional army which we have. It has always seemed to me that the officers of the army should be pretty much on the same basis as civil servants, and I think it is at least open to question whether fulltime soldiers, members of the permanent forces, while such, should take active part in party political discussions. I think there is a good deal to be said against it. They have never done so in the past, any more than members of the permanent civil service are allowed to do it. But with that reservation I agree that members of the citizen army should be free to express political opinions and that members of political parties should engage in political discussion without prejudicing their position in the army.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I do not know that I should take part in a discussion of the estimates which are now before the house, but in listening to the story which has just been told I thought that something should be said with regard to the matter itself which is under

Demobilization-Army
discussion. In the first place, I cannot think of any reason why a man with the record which has just been given to this house should have any objection whatsoever to having his name presented. I think he should consider it an honour to have his name presented anywhere.
May I say that I withheld it on my own initiative. I am quite prepared to give the name. It is Captain Leo Heaps.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Well, with the name before the house, most hon. members who have been here for some years will know of course that he is the son of a previous member of this house, as has been stated. But it was not that in particular that I wished to bring to the attention of the house. It is the fact that, one can check the record of any organization in this country, army or otherwise, and find young men who have entered upon a profession or into an activity in connection with politics, it might be, or in connection with anything else, who in the early stages of their endeavours were not as successful as they were in later years or even in later months. As a matter of fact, one has only to read history to know that men even as great as Lord Clive had some very difficult experiences in the army and elsewhere, though eventually they had a very enviable record and one which made them famous in history. And so there is nothing at all unusual about that.
But the suggestion has been made-and I presume it was for that reason that the speech was delivered-that someone somewhere objected to men being in the army who had the views that were held by persons such as Mr. Heaps, while he was in this house-and I presume his son holds similar views. All one needs to do is to check the records over a very short time to know that there has been no such thing in the army during this war. There may be individuals who for one reason or another were barred from making advancement in certain directions in certain places, but anyone who examines the records knows that some of the highest officials of the organization which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldiwell) leads, the C.C.F., have been advanced along the way, in the army and in association with organizations connected with it, without any obstruction whatsoever, when everyone in this country knew their views, not only those who were in the army but those outside it as well. No less a person than one of the members of the government of Saskatchewan had a record in the army, where he was advanced from one position to another. I have no doubt he gave good
service. He went overseas, came back, ran an election and is in the government. Everyone knew what he was before he went away, and everyone knows what he is since his return. I refer to Mr. Sturdy. But there are others even in this house who have advanced views from the floor of the house, very freely from time to time, and who had exactly the same experience in the army, and their views were just as radical as those of any man who has been spoken of this afternoon.
Mr. COLD'WELL: But his views were not radical; that is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Maybe they were not, and that is all the more reason for saying that he was not refused promotion for being radical.
That was the reason given, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Those men who have been advanced in the army were known to be what is called radical. I do not know whether my hon. friend vrould agree that they are radical, but the views he is speaking of, the views held by C.C.F. members in this house and outside, are sometimes spoken of as being radical, and I have never heard that radical views of the C.C.F. ever prevented anyone getting anywhere in the army.
Just from getting into the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As a matter of fact the main complaint that you hear from time to' time is that there are far too many of them in the army in different parts. My friends over on the other side of the house have been, bragging, ever since the war started, that they could command more votes in the army than anyone else.
More of the privates.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
If they could command more votes than anyone else I do not see that anyone was being obstructed on entering the army and proceeding along the line of advancement as rapidly as others who had other political views.
I do not know why the speech was made; I can conceive of its being made except for one purpose only, namely, a political purpose, and therefore I made the observations which I have made as a check upon it.

Mr. Chairman, the
speech was not made for a political purpose.
Yes, it was.

The speech was made with deliberate intent to do something else. It was made with the deliberate intent to put
Demobilization-Army

before the committee the idea that if we are to have an army in Canada, let it be a citizens' army where there is freedom of speech, and freedom of discussion. That was the object I had in mind. I thought I could attain it best "by putting this case before the committee. Let me say to the minister that he missed my point in that regard. I rose to .make that point, and if I did not succeed in making it, well, then, I should regard my remarks as having failed in the objective I had in mind, because I think that in the future it is important that we shall have men and women in the army who, if war comes, understand what they are fighting for and the implications of what they are fighting for.
The minister himself says that in the small professional army there might be some reason why the men who are in that army should not take part in active political discussions, because they are in the position of civil servants. I myself have always wondered why civil servants should be debarred from discussing political affairs. The more we get socialized industry and socialized organizations, even under the present government, the more we shall find that a large number of our .ablest citizens are debarred from taking an active interest in the affairs of their country. To my mind that is all wrong.

Do you advocate
socialism?

I advocate what I
believe to be right.
So everybody should .shut up?
No. Of course, this lion, gentlemen apparently imagines that a loud voice makes up for everything else. But I want to tell him that behind the voice you have to have some ideas; and those of us-

You are not very
effective.

Those of us who are called socialists at least have some ideas; otherwise we would not be content to be in the organization of which we are a part. But what I want to impress upon the committee is that in my opinion there should be absolute freedom among our men and women in the armed forces. I know there has been an unwritten rule-I believe it is unwritten-that in an officers' mess, for example,'politics shall not be discussed. I am not sure whether religion is not in the same category.
And women.

There may be other matters, too.
tMr. Coldwell.l
Did not that apply during the war?	[DOT]

Yes, I am told that so far as politics were concerned it did apply during the war. In my opinion, if we are to have a citizens' army-and it is the only kind of army we should tolerate in this country- it should be under the control of the representatives of the people, and not under the control of any military hierarchy. All Canadians must have freedom of speech and freedom of discussion.

I find myself in substantial agreement with what the leader of the C.C.F. has just said. I know this may be a surprise to many hon. members; nevertheless I know something of the case which he has just mentioned. At one time I happened to be in the branch of the service which he mentions, and I happen to know the group in Camp Borden which were having these discussions. I attended some of those meetings. They were led by various officers. At one time they were led effectively by one of the padres at Camp Borden; they discussed political problems, and covered a very wide field. Naturally a report of those meetings was submitted to the district officers commanding and to National Defence Headquarters; and these meetings probably horrified the permanent force senior officers, because possibly rightly and possibly not, they considered policies as something that was never discussed in military life. I do not know that there was an adverse report made, but there was a great deal of adverse comment about the meetings of those groups at Camp Borden. The report came to me, and being a politician myself I could see no possible-
A statesman.
Oh, oh.
Where?

And certainly I have
made no attempt at any time, whether in the service or out of it, to withhold any condemnation or disapproval of actions of the past and present government. But this was something new; those discussion groups were something that was unknown to the permanent force officers. I believe that they did a lot of good. I believe they showed what the troops were thinking: I believe they gave the staff a far more useful cross-section of the opinion in the army than a great many other methods which were tried to evaluate morale.
The war just concluded was not like the previous war. In a camp such as Borden the officers do not know what the men are thinking; in a training camp, where the soldiers are constantly passing through, the officers have very little opportunity to get to know the men. There will be a draft going through every two or three weeks or even oftener. Training camp life differs greatly from regimental life where the officers know the men intimately. I believe those discussions, even though sometimes they were quite frankly radical, were a good thing, and I should like to commend the leader of the C.C.F. party for having brought this subject to the attention of the committee. This is one of the few occasions on which I have agreed with that party at all. We had a citizen army, and though we wore uniforms we were still citizens of the country, and could not be expected to refrain from expressing our political views.

It is hard to be seen down at this end of the chamber, Mr. Chairman; this is my fourth attempt to get the floor, and at last I have succeeded. First I want to say
that some remarks were made from the other side of the house yesterday to the effect that it rather seemed there were not many members on this side of the house speaking on national defence matters. There are a few over here, such as the hon. member for Fraser Valley and myself, who are inclined to be a little bit shy, but after a while we will improve.
I think we all agree that during the war the Canadian army was very efficient. The first Canadian corps marched side by side with the eighth army, and was quite as efficient as that army, by which it was highly regarded. It formed an integral part of that wronderful fighting force, which will go down through the ages as one of the most famous in the Briitsh empire. The Canadian army was also part of the 21st army group in northwest Europe, where it made an enviable reputation for itself. It will be known wherever the 21st army group is known; I think we can all agree on that.
I want to get down to a few basic facts, because after all we are really discussing these estimates and I do not think it is fair to digress too much, since time is precious. One question I should like to bring up is the matter of military law, which I think in its application should be streamlined in relation to active service. This is something I always hoped to have a chance to have discussed in this House of Commons, not knowing I would be able to do it myself. During a campaign, officers should not be called from duty with fighting units to act on courts martial. There should be mobile courts composed of men trained for the job, men who could be sent out to units from time to time to get unit training if that should be considered necessary to advance their general knowledge as far as dealing out jurisprudence is concerned. I believe that if we had these mobile courts of inquiry or courts martial we would find that the justice meted out would be more equal. I maintain that officers who are not fully conversant with the procedure of courts martial and who are suddenly called in to sit on a court are rather at a loss; I believe most of the former officers in this house will agree with that statement. So I hope the legal procedure as it refers to the army will be streamlined in the near future.
One other point I should like to bring up, which I mentioned in another place to-day, is in relation to the term "brass hats". We all use that phrase and have a good laugh. I know most people use it to refer to a certain type of officer, but I maintain that expression should not be used so generally, because the so-called brass hats with whom I have had anything to do have been very able leaders, men I have been glad to follow through the
163S
Demobilization-Army

campaigns in Italy and northwest Europe. They really knew their jobs. Many of them have worked their way up, some even coming from the ranks. Therefore we should not use that term so generally in this house and have it get into the press, because then the rear rank private, the gunner or the sapper, as the case may be, reads in the newspapers about the brass hats and says, "Those are the fellows leading us." In all fairness I ask hon. members to be very careful in using that phrase.
Then I want to say that you must trust your officers who are on the ground. If officers who are actually in the theatre of war or, as is the case now, in the army of occupation in Europe, make suggestions, let us not throw those suggestions out and say they only come from brass hats. Of course this house can throw out any suggestion it chooses, but we should give them due consideration because otherwise we simply undermine the discipline and strength of the men who are carrying on the administration overseas. Anyone who has had the control of troops in foreign countries, particularly when they have come out to rest after hard fighting, realizes what a difficult problem it is to deal with those men. You must be tactful; you must be firm; you must be a doctor, a lawyer, an Indian chief; you have to be everything in order to keep those men happy and out of trouble. If the officers who are overseas send back suggestions, as they have in connection with this point system, certainly those suggestions should be considered. Yesterday we were told the names of the officers who had worked out the point system. They are all officers for whom I have ' the highest regard, and for whom I think everyone in this house has a great deal of respect. I do not say their suggestions should become hard and fast rules, but following the request of hon. members opposite the minister nas stated that he will inquire into this matter. If the overseas officers still say the point sj'stem is satisfactory, then let us examine it very carefully before we disagree with them.
I am not saying it is right or wrong; I think the minister is following the proper course in referring the matter to the officers actually concerned, upon the suggestion coming from the other side of the house.
Now I should like to say a wrord or two regarding the future of the army. I believe we must develop our N.P.A.M. along modernized lines, and must consider it a necessary part of the army. This is a very important matter, and these N.P.A.M. units should not be run like clubs. I know there is a certain amount of club life in connection with them, rMr. Baker.]
but they must be efficient, well trained units; they must be provided with proper training centres, and we must not stint their supplies of ammunition and other types of equipment. I feel this can be done. I also hope the 'Canadian army will continue its research work, because that is most necessary. The allied armies picked up a good many pointers from Jerry in this last war, and that should not be the case; we should always be one jump ahead of any potential enemies, if at all possible.
With regard to political discussions in the army, I was interested in what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had to say. But political discussions as such, that is straight party discussions, as I see it cannot be permitted in a permanent force, inasmuch as these men are servants of the crown and that army is fighting for the crown, not for any political party. We have seen what has happened in Central and South American countries when politics have become rife in the army; inevitably there has been trouble. The same thing happened in Russia many years ago, as will be remembered by anyone who has read Russian history. Therefore I say political discussions as such should mot take place in any mess, mess hall or other meeting place of that kind; but I do maintain that you can discuss the issues of the day, as we did in Europe. We had what we called the A.B.C.A., which is familiar to many hon. members; that is the army bureau of current affairs, which covered a broad field in a most interesting way. I found that if officers really wanted to do their work and took an interest in their men, the men enjoyed it. They might ask questions which the officers could not answer, but they would try to get the answers later. Then we also had "Canadian Current Affairs" sent to us. I think all troops should be encouraged to study political issues in a broad'way, but we must not bring the party element into it, so long as those men are in the employ of the crown. I believe there is no need to emphasize that point further. In view of what has happened to political armies in other countries it must be realized that that is a dangerous procedure, whereas in the British army they did not have that trouble. Politics, religion and women's names are good things to be left out of the mess.
Having covered the main points in which I was interested, I would ' also say that we should try to have more French-speaking officers in the Canadian army. I am not so sure that I agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Bonaventure that French-speaking Canadians should have a separate military

Demobilization-Army
college. If that were done, it seems to me that instead of getting together we would drift apart. It could be made compulsory that a military college be bilingual, but if we were to set up two separate colleges we would have-two separate establishments; we would not be getting together at all. I offer this only as a suggestion-and I hope my suggestions have been constructive.

I had not intended to take part in this debate, and in saying that I believe I am following the example of many hon. members in the chamber who then have launched into forty-minute speeches. I must frankly say, however, that I am baffled by army procedure. My own service has acted in a sensible and logical manner and, as an air force man, I am glad to follow it. Further, I should be quite content to leave these army estimates to the many military authorities in the house, whose numbers apparently have been greatly increased since the last election.
Last night I was sitting here quietly, minding my own business and keeping my mouth shut-
That is strange.

However, the comments of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and the hon. member
for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) have placed me in the debate ; they have urged that I declare my stand on repatriation of these N.R.M.A. personnel.
As the committee knows, during the conscription debate I expressed positive views in respect of this so-called two-army army. I stated last fall, and I still say, that I do' not believe in a system of that kind, and especially at this time I think that any system which permits the return of N.R.M.A. soldiers who have been sent overseas-whether they have gone active or remained N.R.M.A. soldiers-ahead of volunteers, is wrong. This afternoon I have read this pamphlet on army points score, and, as I said earlier, I am even more baffled than ever by this apparently very ' complicated score system.
In my speeches on military matters in the house in the last five years I have at all times urged, in the interests of all men in the services, that there be a certain consistency in the conditions of service. Last year I recited at length the advantages gained by the men who served in the air force, as compared with those gained by men serving in the army and navy. I argued, of course, that the army and navy should lift their standards.
This matter of repatriation for air force personnel has been handled in a very simple
manner, and one which is consistent with the accepted policy of the Department of Veterans Affairs. There they pay $7.50 a month gratuity for volunteer service in Canada and $15 per month for service overseas-a one-to-two point score: And so it is in the air force. We give one point for home service and two points for overseas. I assume it would be preferable if we could make a provision for, first of all, combat service. But, even in the air force, where it is generally accepted that service in aircrew is combat service and service in ground crew is non-combatant, that system does not apply, because there are ground crew who have seen more combatant service than have some members of air crew. And so that broad principle which has been so well accepted by the troops as a ground for gratuities I think might well have been adopted not only by the air force-as it has been-but by the army, too, as a general policy, subject of course to the conditions of need of long-service men in key positions from time to time, and of course subject to the fact that returning army units as regiments, such as the Seaforths of Vancouver, is a most desirable thing.
I do not believe any N.R.M.A. soldier should receive any points at all for the time he spent in Canada as a conscript. I am quite sure that if the army would adopt this system, most of the present complaints against the return of these N.R.M.A. men overseas, who have piled up a large point score because of long service as conscripts in Canada, could be avoided.
I have one other suggestion-one which has already been made. On some occasions I have claimed that N.R.M.A. personnel were of no use to Canada in a time of war. Now I think they could be used even to a greater degree, perhaps, than the fighting troops. They could be used as occupational troops, because they have occupied Canada with great ease for the last four years. I say they are far better fitted to serve as occupational troops in Europe to-day. They certainly are lacking in points, if we wipe out the points for service in Canada, but they have had long military training-we cannot say they are untrained. I should like to see the minister announce a set policy of sending the remaining 35,000 overseas, so that he might not release them to industry, and so that he might return our low-point volunteers home as quickly as possible.
Before taking my seat I should like to make one further remark about the remarks of my
Demobilization-Army

young and gallant friend from Kamloops. Speaking last night the hon. member referred to me in this way:
, Mr. Fulton: How does the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) feel about it? We used to get his letters-and I am not criticizing him personally-saying how much the government was going to do for the men who were carrying the country's burdens in the field of battle.
I believe certain hon. members might have gained the impression that I had been publicly canvassing the troops with political dodgers on behalf of the government. Let me assure the house that that is far from the truth. During my own service in Libya I found that members in my squadron knew absolutely nothing about what the government was planning for us, and I pledged myself that upon my return I would see to it that, every member in my squadron should receive government literature on the subject. With that in mind I sent that literature to every soldier from my constituency, and to many in the Seaforths. I sent particularly that little booklet "Back to Civil Life", and various publications of the soldier settlement board, showing what the government was doing. Hon. members opposite will remember that my remarks were more critical than laudatory wdien I spoke last year.
I should like to correct the impression gained by the hon. member for Kamloops that these letters were of a political nature. I was pleased however to find that he had remembered them. Apparently he prized [DOT] them so highly that he still treasures and remembers them. For that I am grateful.
Then, I have one further reference which the young member made-and perhaps I should not be so patronizing, because I am only a little senior to him, but to become patronizing is an easy habit. to develop. I refer to his comment at page 1613 of Hansard, where he is reported to have said:
I wish to associate myself most wholeheartedly with what has just been said by the hon. member for Vancouver South, and to say how much more I feel as I felt sometimes when we were overseas, that it is nice to know there are one or two individuals in this House of Commons who have the interests of the men overseas at heart

As a member of the house who is only slightly senior to the hon. member for Kamloops I should like to assure him that it has been my experience during my five years in the house that it has not been only one or two members who had at heart the interests of the fighting men, but almost every member, without exception, on the government side, among the Tories, the C.C.F. and the Social Credit. All of them had the interests of the

fighting men at heart. And, more than that, they felt that way, whether or not they had served in the armed forces. I hope the hon. member will take that assurance from me. ' I do not say this in any spirit of reproof, but I say it as something which comes from one British Columbian to another.
I know that on occasions in the house he has been chided by the Prime Minister and by other senior members. I have great sympathy with him in that connection, because in my first session I had the same experience. The hon. member and myself have a great deal in common, perhaps more than the committee realizes. We are both British Columbians, we have the same educational background, we are both veterans, we both have a certain confidence in that we defeated sitting members of this house, and we both in a sense have been in the opposition. At that time I sat in almost the same seat as the hon. member, and when you face the government you are a little more critical than when you sit with them. I can assure him that I have great sympathy with him. However, he may not fully appreciate that sympathy so I would like to go just a little further. If five years from now, when the next parliament of 1950 is sitting, another bright Rhodes scholar comes down from the west and sits in this house and-with all the arrogan-ce Of youth and the assurance that comes from membership in the Oxford Union he proceeds to pontificate in lordly fashion on all public issues, then I hope the hon. member for Kamloops will reflect then as I have reflected now, "Was I really like that my first session?"

I can assure the hon. member for Vancouver North that I take in very good part the remarks he has made this afternoon. However, there are one or two mis-impressions, if I may so refer to them, that I should like to correct. Any little facility that I may have in this house is certainly not derived from the Oxford Union. I want that to be cleared up at the outset. As a matter of fact it was the members of my college who went into the Oxford Union and removed a certain page from the book.
With regard to the question of the letters sent out by the hon. member for Vancouver North, may I say that I recall them with a great deal of pleasure. Apparently he does not realize the efficiency with which his organization worked, because I received a letter addressed to me personally. I thought I had been careful in my remarks to point out that the hon. member himself was not promising anything. He was, as he pointed out, simply saying what the government had

Demobilization-Army
in mind in bringing to our attention the statement which had been made as to what was being done for those .overseas. If the misapprehension existed in his mind or in the mind of any hon. member of this house that I intended to say he was making promises, and I do not even say that the promises are not going to be kept-
They have been kept.

-I am glad to have that misapprehension removed.
I should like to say a few words with regard to my statement last night. Attention has been focussed, partly by the hon. member for Vancouver North, on the first part of my remarks. I said, as reported on page 1613 of Hansard:
-there are one or two individuals in this House of Commons who had the interests of the men overseas at heart-[DOT]
As I set out immediately after I had made that first remark, I was referring to the hon. member for Vancouver South. I then went on to say:
-and who would not be howled down, as an attempt was made to do to-night when they rose to speak about them.
As I pointed out later to the hon. member for Fraser Valley, I had made no distinction. Perhaps I was less than generous in saying '"one or two individuals". As I explained to him, I made that remark with a certain thing in mind and I wish now to make up for any lack of generosity on my part on that occasion by saying there were certainly more than one or two members, and I know full well there were members on all sides of the house, who had the interest of the men overseas at heart.

Mr. Chairman, I have heard a great deal of discussion on these estimates, and I find it hard to agree that in most cases the discussion has been relevant to the estimates under consideration. Often it has been on specific points of the estimates, but in many instances it has had nothing to do with the estimates or with army matters. Hon. members have engaged in personalities and the discussion of other points. I will -state at the outset that I shall try to confine myself to the army estimates on the basis of the broad presentation brought down by the minister.
Much of what I have heard so far has been criticism, so I should like to start off with the unique statement that I think the minister has done a good job and I think the Department of National Defence has done a good job. I have no doubt the minister has done the best job possible with -the information
available to him. As you all know, when you approach any problem you have to take the facts at your disposal. The minister has said that he cannot complete arrangements for the post-war army until our commitments abroad are known. That is what I refer to when I say that he has done the best he could with the information available to him at this time.
We have heard a great deal of discussion about the repatriation system. I think there could have been improvements here; I think that we should have given more weighting to the man who had been in combat, but we must recognize the fact that well over 100,000 -I think the correct figure is around 110,000- troops have been returned since V-E day. The men of the services are being released at a rate in excess of 2,000 a day, which is pretty fair.
I was particularly pleased that the minister in his statement cleared up certain points about the interim army. I made the statement previously that the programme as it stood was not good enough because it would not encourage the right type of man to enter the service.
I am glad the minister has stated that he will outline a firm policy on the army by March 31, and if at that time those in the interim army are not satisfied with conditions, they will be released from their terms of service. I think that will be helpful in bringing a better type of man into the service.
The minister went on to say that pay and allowance would be considered carefully, that the pay to be given to the man in the service would be good pay. I think we should go one step farther and place equal emphasis on the fact that in addition to being well paid, the service must be an efficient service. The two go hand in hand. We must be prepared to pay if we want the right type of people. We have to sell to the public the idea that service in the armed forces is service to the people, and we have to be prepared to pay on a scale comparable to what a man with corresponding ability would get in industry or some other civilian occupation. The minister in introducing his estimates set forth one condition of service which to my mind is indefinite. He said, as reported on page 1135 of Hansard:
Anyone who has been accepted for the interim force will be accepted into the permanent force, subject of course to continued good conduct, satisfactory medical category and military efficiency of the individual.
Knowing something of the attitude of the soldier to the interim army, I cannot say that that statement as it reads in Hansard is selective enough. I do not believe it will screen the more desirable types from the less desirable. I think that the minister will take care
Demobilization-Army

of that situation and that we can rely on him to get the right type of man into the service, notwithstanding the apparent openness of that condition.
As to the size of the permanent force, the minister has stated that it will be between
20,000	and 25,000, all ranks. I am not of course in a position to say whether that is large enough or whether it is too large. I am one of those who believe that we should have a reasonably large permanent force. I do not believe that the development of new weapons, even including the atomic bomb, will greatly reduce the demand for holding forces such as will be required in the event that there is another war.
' The minister announced these figures to indicate what we may expect in our establishments. But I should like to make this point, that I do not think the statement of over-all establishments means much to the individual. What the individual wants to know is what job he will have to do and how much he will be paid for doing that job. I would recommend, therefore, that the minister at the earliest possible date break down these overall figures into basic unit establishments and attempt to bring the strengths of all units up to establishments as soon as possible.
There is another clause which is set forth on page 1133 of Hansard, where it is stated: Resumption of university or equivalent higher education has also been made a basis for immediate discharge and while this may be extended to a limited degree with respect to secondary schools, it does not include resumption of technical or business training.
I think the extension of the concession to secondary school training is well worth while. Several such instances have been referred to me and I in turn have mentioned them to the minister. It is probably more important to a man who left high school to be returned to continue his high school training, than is the remainder of his course to a man who has probably only one year to go at college. That is a very important concession on the part of the minister, and one with which I am pleased.
Again, the minister set forth on page 1134 of Hansard several reasons for which extended leave with pay and. allowances could be granted. Among those he lists compassionate leave, farm leave, hog, dairy and beef production and so on, and at the end of it he says "et cetera". I notice, having due regard to my constituency, that fishing is not listed there; I hope it is included in the "et cetera", and I have reason to believe that the minister will regard it in that spirit.

A few nights ago the hon. member for St. John-Albert, in speaking of the navy, said it was his desire that we should benefit from what we went through at the outset of this war. In other words, he recalled the difficulties we ran into in getting production under way; our lack of tools and facilities of various kinds, and asked the minister what steps were being taken to avail ourselves of the experience gained. I can say a word in that respect with regard to the army. I know the position in which we found ourselves in the early stages; and we did have difficulties. The chief of the general staff, somewhat less than a year ago as I recall, circularized all staff officers of N'.D.H.Q. of the rank of grade II and higher, and asked them to place on record any suggestions they might have with a view to avoiding the recurrence of similar conditions. In the corps with which I am associated, being a technical corps, we were fully aware of the technical problems involved. We placed on record suggestions which were based on our experience in the early part of this war. The general staff has acknowledged them, has them on record, and has studied them, and I am sure I can say that so far as the army is concerned something has been done to benefit from that experience.
The field of research is one on which I should like to say a few words. My colleague the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmou&~ Clare stated that we should have a broad programme of research. I endorse that now as I have on other occasions. In the light of the war it is difficult to overemphasize the part which resea'rch has played, particularly, for example, in atomic energy and the field of electronics. I believe thaf the government will have to take a more vigorous part in coordinating the programme of this country, than it has done heretofore. I can well picture that we shall come to the point where the government will find it expedient to coordinate the research programmes of the national research council, for example, private enterprise, army research, and so on. But when we attempt to commit the army to a programme of research we must be somewhat careful in our definition of what research is. We must break down research into twro broad classes, one fundamental or basic research and the other practical research. We can illustrate that well by the atomic bomb. It has been known for ten or fifteen years that it was a reasonable proposition to split the atom. It was known, too, that there was enormous potential energy in an atom. But,
I submit, until the time it was known that an atom could be split and that the potential energy could be realized, it was a matter of

Demobilization-Army
fundamental or basic atomic research, and it is difficult to conceive that the army should have been in on it at that stage. However, once we knew that the atom could be split by practical means and that the energy could be made available for purposes of war, it was conceivable that the army should play an important part in the research programme.
Another interesting item in that connection which I should like to place before the committee is the proximity fuse, or, as it is sometimes known, the variable time fuse. A great deal of publicity, particularly in the United States, has been given to this fuse. In the last copy of Lije I saw an article explaining the operation of the proximity fuse. My point in bringing this up is that I think it serves to illustrate Canada's important contribution to that field of research as well as to delineate the two phases of research which I have attempted to outline, namely basic research on the one hand and practical research on the other. The proximity fuse is just a development of the electro-magnetic principle. The idea as I understand it was conceived in England, when research men came to the conclusion that if they could fit a radio set into the fuse of a shell and have that radio set emit signals and receive them back, if they were reflected by an obstructing medium of some kind, that at . a predetermined intensity of the received signal the fuse would trigger off and the shell would explode. That idea as I say was conceived in England, and was brought to this continent by a technical mission, because it was realized that out here, in the United States and Canada, there were more resources which could be applied to its development. Accordingly the , United States and Canada went to work on it and they found it to be a practical proposition. They developed small tubes, the right type of battery, condensers, and so on, and eventually the fuse took shape. The Canadian army kept a very watchful eye on that development. Although they did not play an active part as army personnel, they saw the potentialities in it; they gave every encouragement to the project, and I understand that they financed it to a large extent in Canada. To illustrate the important part which Canada has played, and for which I do not believe it has received full credit, I understand that the first proximity fuse -was assembled and fired in Canada.
Another field of research in which I think the Canadian army has from the outset taken a leading role is operational research. To that end the Canadian army has carried out cold weather tests for a number of years at places like Camp Shilo, Valcartier, Churchill and so on, and in the past two years it has
run operational programmes which have put to the test in operational roles the data accumulated in previous years. It is common knowledge that, last year they ran three separate exercises, one of which was known as exercise Eskimo, a dry cold operational exercise involving approximately battalion strength, and run in northern Saskatchewan, north of Prince Albert. The second was known as exercise Polar Bear, which was a wet cold exercise-an operational exercise again-run in northern British Columbia. The third was exercise Lemming, which was a quick dash inland from Churchill last winter. All three of these exercises were eminently successful. They were watched very closely by observers from most allied nations but Canada played the part of carrying them out. The Department of National Defence deserves a great deal of credit for these exercises, which have undoubtedly contributed in great measure to the knowledge of operations in cold weather. That, I think, we can consider in the same light as remarks made in connection with the port of Churchill, wherein it was suggested that Canada should . know more about cold weather operations.
The army has played an outstanding role in the development of Canada in that respect, and it is continuing to play that outstanding role. Hon. members will have seen in the press recently that during the coming winter there will be ' another operational exercise known as operation Musk-Ox, which will start at Churchill and terminate at Edmonton. It will go through the Arctic regions, covering a distance of some three thousand miles.
These are valuable contributions and, as I say, I feel justified in supporting the Department of National Defence and in opposing all the criticism I have heard in the last two or three days. I am one of those who have spent some time at national defence headquarters in this war; and in regard to the statements made earlier in the afternoon about Frenchspeaking officers I can say that at no time, in my opinion, has any discrimination been shown at [DOT] national defence headquarters against French-speaking officers. There are, of course, certain positions into which you cannot put an English-speaking officer in this country; conversely there are certain vacancies that, cannot be filled by French-speaking officers. These conditions we must and do recognize. But I believe I am safe in saying that there has been no discrimination at national defence headquarters. Certainly there has not been in any department with which I have been associated.
In conclusion, I would say that in my opinion the Minister of National Defence and
Demobilization-Army

the department have both done a good job, and I for one have appreciated the open and frank way in which the minister has placed his estimates before the house.
Mr. PEARIvES: I did not intend to say anything at this moment because I shall have a good deal to say before these estimates are passed.
