I have had a great deal to do with the selection of officers, both those from the ranks who were seeking commissions, and the promotion of officers to senior rank and appointment, and I thought my silence might be misinterpreted if I did not just say a word in connection with the discussion which took place earlier this afternoon. I believe that the principle was so thoroughly understood by all commanders of officers training corps and of all units, that selection for commissions and selection for promotion was to be based on merit and merit only, that it was impossible for any officer or young man seeking a commission to be discriminated against because of any political leanings he might have. Furthermore, I know of a great many cases in which those who were charged with the responsibility of making the selections may have made mistakes because, as the Minister of Agriculture said, young men in the earlier stages of training did not always show the promise that developed later. But I go farther and say that after thirty years experience with the permanent force, in which I have served in appointments under two hon. members in this house who were holding the portfolio of Minister of National Defence, to my personal knowledge I have never seen any case in which the political leanings or supposed political leanings of any officer have been either beneficial or detrimental to him. I might say that at one time I was accused of having political leanings myself, but it did not affect my promotion or otherwise.
Regarding the suggestion that perhaps permanent force officers were retarding the free discussion of general topics within the army during this war, I should like to dispel any thought along those lines, because we had in the army overseas and in the army in Canada regular discussions and padres' hours under what was known as the army bureau of current affairs; I know that the two men who were most instrumental in promoting these discussions were General McNaughton and General
(Mr. Winters.]
Simmonds, and great latitude was given to all ranks when discussing problems affecting current affairs.
I am pleased to say that when I was overseas my senior educational officer, the gentleman who was responsible for promoting these study groups, was one who now holds a cabinet position in Saskatchewan. I pay the highest tribute to Mr. Sturdy. I knew what his political leanings were at that time but it never made the slightest bit of difference, and I know that Mr. Sturdy did not attempt to introduce any party politics into the discussions which he carried out. Those discussions were carried out on broad lines and I can speak highly of the work he has done.

In the event that the
political side of this discussion has been concluded, we might turn to another subject. I wish to make some reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg who was so very happy with the policy of the government, had so much praise for it, and suggested that there had been too much criticism of it. In his place in this house probably the hon. member has a duty not to be critical. In our place over here on this side of the house we possibly have a duty to be critical.

I might say that I put
myself under no obligation at all. I think that should be on record.

That is quite understood. I would certainly prefer to be able to fill the air with my praises of the work of the minister, particularly since the subjects which we are discussing are very close to my heart. However, I find I cannot do that because of the prevailing attitude which the government appear to. adopt of refraining from informing the house and this committee exactly what their policy is. Since that is the position they take, I am afraid it will be necessary for us on this side to be continuously critical. With these remarks I take up the heavy burden.
When I say that the government has not announced its policy I am going to speak of the army of occupation. It is quite unaccountable to me that in making his statement on the estimates the minister gave us no information whatever on the policy of the government in respect of that very important force. Nothing was said about its future. Nothing was said about the policy to be followed with regard to the force itself or with regard to the maintenance of it and its reinforcements.
Since the minister has not seen fit to explain anything to the committee with regard to this occupation force, I should like to place before the committee some facts with regard to it.

Demobilize tion-Army
First of all, I should like to refer to this booklet entitled, "After Victory in Europe." On page 4, under the heading, "Our job is not yet finished," we find the purpose of the army of occupation laid down. We find there the following:
This time there will be no clear-cut, immediate ending to our contact with Germany and the Germans. While the nazis are being hunted to their lairs, Germany must be disciplined in the ways of peace. Canada, as one of the united nations, is pledged to play her part in educating Germany to fit that country to take its place in the society of decent nations. This will be an important task of the. Canadian occupation force.	[DOT]
That seems to me to be a very good description of its purpose, and a very fine and worthy purpose it is too. I suggest that it is important to Canada that that force be maintained until the job is done. The maintenance of that force in Europe until that job is done is just as important to this country and to this committee as was the approval the other day of the united nations charter. That is one of the reasons why I find it so strange that no mention was made by the minister of the army of occupation.
Let me now turn from the purpose of the army of occupation and refer to its composition. The strength of the army of occupation was placed on Hansard at page 603, and again the other night by the hon. member for Vancouver South at page 1613. I do not propose to go through all those figures again, but I wish to point out these significant facts. Of the twenty thousand men in that army nine per cent are N.R.M.A. troops, thirty-one per cent are general service troops who showed a preference for the army of occupation, and sixty per cent are general service troops who specifically elected not to serve in the army of occupation unless they must.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is changing all the
time, as my hon. friend knows.

The minister says that it is changing all the time. Perhaps he can give us the actual figures this afternoon. Of the sixty per cent that I mentioned-this was on September 1-twenty per cent of the total, namely 4500, were soldiers who had had six months battle service. That is the composition of the force. At about the same date, August 29, we had in the N.R.M.A. force in Canada some 35,276 all ranks. At that time there were, in addition, undoubtedly a considerable number of young soldier volunteers with very low point scores. I have lumped together those N.R.M.A. personnel in Canada and the young soldier volunteers because of the principle enunciated the other day by the hon. member for Nanaimo, that if there is to be no two-army system in Europe there
should be no two-army system here. I suggest that the principle he enunciated is a wholesome one. I use the word "wholesome" advisedly, because I think the best description of the government's continuing man-power policy is that it is an unwholesome policy.
Some hon. members may wonder why I have mentioned the strength of the army of occupation alongside the strength of the N.R.M.A. personnel in Canada. I do so, of course, because there is a decided connection. One of the things that we will want to find out in the discussion on these estimates is whether this government believes that there is any connection between the twenty thousand men in the army of occupation and the
35,000	N.R.M.A. men in Canada. We feel that there is a great connection; that they are interchangeable, and we want to know whether the government thinks they are interchangeable; but I intend to come back to that.
I wish to speak for a moment about the army of occupation and the troops over there. That army is doing a very good job and a very necessary one, in carrying out the principle that I have referred to in this little booklet. It would not concert at all with Canada's position as a nation were we not to maintain that army of occupation in Germany, just as some of us feel that it does not concert with Canada's position as a nation in the world that we are not now represented in the occupation forces in the Pacific. Although the job must be done, we must think 'also of the men who are there to do Canada's job for her. No one will suggest that it is an easy job. It is not a job very many of them sought; it is not an exciting job. It is a job done under difficult circumstances, in the presence of a' hostile or at least unfriendly people, certainly in the presence of a surly people, as I know full well; and at best it is a routine job. None of these things makes a man very happy to stay there. It is also a job in which a man is cut off from home, and above all it is a job for which the men did not bargain when they enlisted for service. These men will do their duty, but sixty per cent of them by their own election want to come home, and the government must accede to that request and bring them home if at all possible.
Of course that is not possible now; the shipping situation does not permit it and will not permit it until after next March or April, when the other divisions are home. That is perfectly understood; but after March that obstacle will be overcome. Another reason I found it unaccountable that we had heard nothing of the policy up to the present was
Demobilization-Army

that this matter cannot wait until the next session of parliament before being decided. If it is impossible to do anything for these men before next March, certainly it will be possible to do something for them immediately after that; and if we are to replace them, or replace those who do not wish to continue to serve, the policy must be decided now. The replacements must be found and trained now, if they are not already trained, and they must be ready to go over. They could be in England while the fourth division is still coming back, so that there would be no delay at all and any ships available after the return of the fourth division could be used to continue the stream of those 12,000 all ranks who do not want to serve in the army of occupation. That is why we must determine the policy at this time, and I say to the committee that it must be determined in this parliament. It is not only the minister and the government who have a duty toward those men. We in this committee have just as great a duty, and it is in an attempt to carry out that duty I am speaking at the present time.
I am going to suggest to the minister that before the conclusion of the debate on these estimates he declare that this government considers N:R.M.A. personnel and young soldiers in Canada as a single force; that there is no distinction between them as, according to his own statement, there is no distinction between them in Europe; that the force in Europe and the force in Canada are qually interchangeable the one with the other, according to their respective point scores; that if there is a man overseas with a point score of 100 and a man in Canada with a point score of 60, let us say, the man with 60 points -should go overseas to take the place of the man with 100 points who wishes to come home. Further, I am going to suggest to him that the time has come when this skeleton in the cupboard, as it was referred to by one hon. member, must be brought out of the cupboard by the government and faced fairly and squarely. They attempted to carry out a policy of no conscription during the war. I do not like to rehash this old issue, but the trouble is we are not rid of it and will never be rid of it until we are finished with the N.R.M.A. The government attempted to refrain from having conscription during the war. Finally they were forced into the position where they had to bring in a limited form of conscription. Then, in an attempt to uphold what they considered to be a voluntary system they gave the troops in Europe this opportunity of reelection. When the troops behaved as everyone except the government knew they would
CMr, Merritt.1
behave and elected not to serve longer, the government went ahead and conscripted the volunteers.
Surely it is time they gave up trying to balance the two policies they have been trying to follow. Surely it is time we had1 one army. Surely it is the only way this army of occupation will ever be properly reinforced and properly relieved of its present duties. There would be one other way in which those men might be brought home, but that is a way which would not commend itself to me at all. However, I wish to mention it to make sure it is brought up once at least. The other way to bring home those men who do not wish to serve in the army of occupation would be to bring home the army of. occupation itself before its job was done. Above everything else, Mr. Chairman, that way must not be taken. Therefore hon. members on this side of the house are very much interested to learn the policy with regard to the army of occupation and the low-point personnel still on strength in Canada.
With that in mind I have some six specific questions I wish to ask the minister. The first one deals with a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen dated October 17, headed "Occupation forces may train peacetime army." I will read just a short part of it:
Canada's occupation division in Germany prob-. ably will be used as training ground for the dominion's peace-time army of 25,000 men.
Then, after omitting a little:
Major General Yokes, commanding the occupation force, has long held the view that the occupation division should be the focal point of any permanent force' to be built up after the war. His view is shared by other senior permanent officers who feel that conditions in northern Germany provide admirable training ground for a regular army.
My first question is, does that press dispatch represent government policy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. As a rule we do not announce government policy through press dispatches.

Then, just so that there may be no' doubt about this, I should like to ask the minister a further question. Has the government considered using the occupation force in Germany as a training ground for the peace-time army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Do you want these questions answered one by one?
As you like.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I thought probably a number of hon. members of the committee might wish to offer some comments on the army of occupation. It might make for more orderly

Demobilization-Army
debate if they did so, and then I could make my statement at the end, but I will do whatever the committee wishes.
As long as the minister will make a note of the questions, I do not want them answered one by one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Oh, yes; I will make a note of them.

My second question is, how long or until what event is it intended to maintain the army of occupation in Europe? My third question is, from what source is it proposed to find immediate reinforcements for the force to replace casualties which may occur from time to time?
My fourth question is, from what source is it proposed to replace, when shipping space is available, those not desirous of continuing to serve in the army of occupation?
Before putting my fifth question I would quote again from the pamphlet "After Victory in Europe" where, at page six, paragraph 14, we find this:
No soldier who has been selected for the Canadian occupation force will lose his chance for thirty clear days' leave at home in Canada, although it may be delayed. Such leave will be given first to those with the longest service and at the earliest possible date. It must be remembered that any arrangements will depend largely upon operational needs for shipping.
My question is, when does the government consider that that occupational leave which seems bo be offered in thfe pamphlet may be commenced?
My sixth and final question requires a word of explanation. Many men in the occupational force have been kept there on the ground1 that they are key men. I agree entirely that one must keep a large number of key men in order to maintain the efficiency of the force. But there is only one ground upon which such a policy can be followed, and at the same time be fair to the men one is keeping, and that is that once one decides that he must keep key men he must set about to train reinforcements to replace those key men.	_
My final question is, what steps have been taken to replace key men; how many key men have been replaced, and when will the minister be in a position to announce to the committee that all key men who have been kept against their wishes have been replaced?

Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers those highly technical questions I should like to say for the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) that I thought of him and of his desk-mate, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) this
afternoon. I was driving to Ottawa with one of my colleagues, on a beautiful day. While driving along I was puzzled, and I had decided upon arrival in the House of Commons to find out if it was the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who successfully canvassed the hon. member for Nanaimo, or if it was the reverse. I was not sure.
Every hon. member in the committee knows that the hon. member for Nanaimo is for conscription. The other day I heard the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard tell the committee that he was in favour of voluntary enlistment for the navy-and I do not think I am misquoting him.	*
May I interrupt the hon. member? I said, voluntary enlistment for the navy, in peace time; and I made that specific reservation. In war time I am in favour of conscription and universal service.

Well, the hon. member for Nanaimo is more successful than the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. Taking for granted what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has said, we must know now if we are at peace or at war. If we are still at war, then the hon. member is in favour of conscription, but if we are at peace, he is in favour of voluntary enlistments - only for the navy. Why only for the navy? I do not know. He establishes a most subtle distinction when he speaks about conscription.
Since the beginning of the war there were difficulties in connection with conscription because the expression was not clearly defined, and because those who advocated total war thought only of a one-sided conscription, and not of a conscription which would be well balanced, and which would form part of a well balanced war effort.
When the hon. member mentioned conscription the other day, he meant, of course, only military conscription as applied to the navy, and left aside the arm-but only in time of peace.
We knew well all the fire-mongers, the jingoes and the junkers we heard in the house during the war, while the hon. member was fighting so gallantly on the shores of France and elsewhere. They were advocating conscription, but in their minds the only man who was doing his duty wTas the man who found himself in any branch of the army. To their minds farmers, railway employees, fishermen, miners, manufacturers of arms and munitions and the men working in the forests were all slackers; they were not doing their bit for the war effort. I am sure my hon. friend will be surprised to hear that.
Demobilization-Army

That was very much so at a time when farmers were brought into the army under false pretences and were kept there by men who did not realize what a total war effort meant. Some of those men were granted leave by the commanding officers of their units on the Pacific coast; but as soon as the hon. member for Nanaimo assumed Pacific command, they were turned down. I am familiar with some cases affecting boys from my constituency. Their duty as good citizens was to work on their farms. However, they were not allowed to return to those farms, with the result that the farms had to be sold and the stock disposed of because the fathers were too old to do the work and needed the help of their robust sons.
These are serious matters. We have to come down to fundamentals. If the hon. member takes it for granted that military conscription is the right thing in time of war, and that those who do their duty are only those who enlist voluntarily, what does he think of those men-perfectly* fit-who enlisted voluntarily in the army on the understanding that they would stay here at headquarters, those men who parade on the sidewalks of Ottawa to such an extent that the sidewalks are not broad enough to hold them? And of course, after the war they would carry the insignia of voluntary enlistment! It will be hard to differentiate these men from men such as my hon. friend who has had a fine war record and from those other soldiers who have not been decorated but who have been in the thick of battle overseas, or even from manufacturers of munitions and arms who have exposed their lives to danger while doing their part of the war effort. Of course they will be the heroes. The girls will run after them and they will have their pictures taken as heroes.
We must come down to realities. Before making subtle distinctions about the policies of the government, we must realize that there is a policy which should be imposed on the government. There should be a clean-up of national defence headquarters with an axe, and one that is well ground. That is the first thing to do. The other day I challenged the members of the committee to come to the defence of the brass hats, but nobody said a word; nobody came to their defence. I complained the other day because an hon. member was referring to certain evils in the abstract form. I said that we must come down to concrete facts; we must come down to personalities; we must come down to names. To start with, we must take the telephone directory in order to see the number of services that have been established during the war. These are

useless services. Why do we hear again the old story of conscription? It is because most of these fellows are brass hats who could not earn their living before the war, and they want this military business to continue as long as possible after the war in order that they may keep their jobs at the expense of the country.
If we are to do something to improve social conditions in the country we must cut off all dead branches; we must uproot the dried fig tree and make a bonfire of it. There is not only an orchard of fig trees, sterile fig trees, in the Department of National Defence; there is a forest primeval of dead wood. They are the people who run the country; their word is the law of the land and it is impossible to get any reform.
I am ready to support those who make constructive suggestions, and here is one constructive suggestion which may look strange. The axe is the tool of the carpenter. Sometimes in order to build something that will resist time, something that is of solid construction, it is necessary to demolish something that has been put on a wrong foundation or is not solid enough. I make that suggestion to my hon. friend. I will have other opportunities to talk about conscription and I will be able to tell my hon. friend how the boys from my county have been insulted after having done such fine duty.
I met Colonel Triquet in Montreal. He comes from my county. As I said the other day to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard,-Colonel Dollard Menard, who was with him at Dieppe, also comes from my county. He is a good French Canadian and there are many like him. My hon. friend knows that is true because he spoke highly of them. During the war the province of Quebec was insulted by certain hon. members who are sitting not far from where the hon. member now sits. It seemed the natural thing to say abominable things about French Canadians.
The farmers were not respected and all those engaged in essential industries were not respected. I have had to fight for them. I have had to fight for the little soldier, the under-dog, so that he would be treated with the consideration he deserves by bullying majors at Petawawa and Camp Borden who were treating men like him as though they were slaves. This still goes on; these men are still being treated in this way. These bullies should be expelled at once from the army. If my hon. friend knew of those cases I know his blood would boil and he would go to the defence of these boys. My intention in rising now was to give him an appetizer of what I will say during this debate about the abominable treatment that has been given to

Demobilization-Army
my fellow citizens from the province of Quebec. The insult was not only to French Canadians; it was to Quebec.
I would remind my hon. friend of what an hon. member said one day from his place in the house. He said that a ship could not leave the port of Quebec because the whole crew was suffering from V.D. or some contagious disease like that. Immediately the medical authorities of the port of Quebec wired to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services and stated that that was untrue. That is what was said right here in this house by the hon. member for Parkdale.
Why attack the province of Quebec like that? Why not give the people of Quebec a chance? We are not just French Canadians; there are some people in Quebec of British origin; there are Jews in Quebec, and there are people of various other races. It was a malicious and wicked attempt to deprecate the province of Quebec in the minds of the people of our sister provinces. I know the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is more broad-minded than that. I would remind him of certain things that are known to all hon. members who were here during the last parliament. They felt indignant. They resented deeply what that hon. member had said. It was felt that he was unworthy of himself when he said things that were so difficult to understand.
It is a burning question. I resented that and it was resented, not only by the people of Quebec but by all fair-minded people and by many members of his own party. This year the tone has changed, I am glad to say, but I must tell my hon. friend that in order to defend our principles, in order to defend the rights of the working man, the man in overalls, we had to suffer insult and calumny. We only wanted to bring back the House of Commons to common sense and to a common understanding.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before I go on, I
wonder whether the minister desires to answer any of the questions which were put to him this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I intimated a little earlier
that I would be glad to make a statement on the occupation forces, following questions by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, but I thought some other members of the committee might like to express their views first.
Perhaps it would help us to hasten the discussion if the minister would make his statement now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think I can do that. The question of the occupation force is, of course, open. One point in the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard with which I am in complete agreement is that provision must be made for the replacement in due course of the men who are serving in the occupation force. As he himself has pointed out, that will not become a practical qurstion until around April or May of next year, because, on present indications as to shipping, we shall not be able to return the remainder of our forces overseas, after making provision for the occupation force, until about that time. But, as he has also quite properly pointed out, provision must be made in advance of that day for the replacements, and I agree with him that plans must be made in advance, and that provision must be started, at the latest, early in the new year to provide for replacement at about the time I have indicated. We do not yet know definitely how long our commitment for occupation troops will last. Of necessity we cannot know_ that. Formally the commitment continues 'until March 31 of next year, but obviously it will not terminate on that day. I think we must proceed on the assumption that it will continue beyond that time.
Does the minister mean 1946 or 1947?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am talking about 1946.
How much longer it will continue I do not know at the moment, and no member of the government knows. That is one of the matters which the Prime Minister will have discussed with the British government and will possibly be discussing with Mr. Truman at the conferences which were referred to this afternoon. It will enable us to make plans on a surer basis when we know a. little more definitely, if we can find out a little more definitely at an early day, how long our occupation commitment is likely to last and how many men we shall need over a period of time.
As to the method of reinforcing the men in the occupation force, that is being given consideration by myself and the officers of the department, and when a decision is reached the policy which the government proposes to adopt will be announced. If the house is in session it will be announced in the session, and if the house is not in session it will be announced in the usual way.
I do not know whether the members of the committee have had time to examine a second pamphlet which I made available to-day. It is entitled "Review of Plan for Repatriation,"
Demobilization-Army

and was issued by headquarters Canadian forces in the Netherlands on September 6, 1945. If they have, they will see that there is a good deal of information in it with respect to the manner in which the occupation force is being made up, and the manner in which the higher point men in the force are being released and replaced by lower point men. Perhaps for the record I might read paragraph 7 of that pamphlet, which will be found on the first page.
I do not think the members of the committee have it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I had a hundred or more
placed on the table to-day, and most of them were distributed. I have one here. That is the first one, and there is a second. I think two hundred of these were placed on the table to-day.
The minister did not have any right to lay them on the table.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It was arranged yesterday that a supply of this pamphlet and the first one, which was issued in May, would be made available to members of the committee, but maybe-

Making them available and laying them on the table are two different matters. Documents which are laid on the table are a matter of record of this house; in that case the officials of the house remove them from the table. Where they went, no one knows.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will withdraw the expression "laid on the table" and substitute, as I said yesterday, "made available to members of the committee." I do not know that we need to be too technical on the matter. The undertaking I gave yesterday was that I would have as many of these pamphlets as were here, made available for the use of the members of the committee to-day, and that is what I tried to do.

If the minister will permit me. it is quite true that none of us is desirous of being too technical; but what actually happened is, they were laid on the table, and staff removed them from the table because they had no right to be on the table. If the minister would see that they were distributed1 by the proper officers of this house, each and all of us would have a copy; but laying them on the table is the prerogative of this parliament and this house and it is not the prerogative of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am afraid there may not be quite enough copies for all the members of the house. I have a note handed to me from 
the assistant clerk of the house that all which were made available were distributed. This particular pamphlet which I hold in my hand was printed overseas. I sent over and had three hundred sent to Canada, and I imagine that most of them were brought here this afternoon. In any event, if we need more we will get them. I believe there are quite a number about and that any hon. member who is really interested can get hold of one. But I was going to read to the committee paragraph 7:
7.	When the 3rd Canadian infantry division C.A.O.F. was formed it was composed of (a) volunteers, (b) non-volunteers with point scores of less than fifty, (c) non-volunteers with scores of fifty and higher. It is the intention that ultimately the C.A.O.F. shall comprise only categories (a) and (b), above.
That is, volunteers, and non-volunteers with point scores of less than fifty.
In forming the occupational force it was necessary to take some non-volunteers to fill establishments in officers, N.C.O.'s. tradesmen and specialists. As far as possible these were selected from personnel with the lowest point scores in the categories required. C.A.O.F. is setting up its own trades schools to train low-score men or volunteers to replace non-volunteer tradesmen and specialists. When all men with scores of less than fifty and C.A.O.F. volunteers at present, in the best general interest, required to serve elsewhere (see paragraphs 12 (b) and 26 below)-
Those deal with certain special categories.
-become available they will be sufficient in numbers to replace non-volunteers in the force.
The release of a small proportion of nonvolunteer officers and N.C.O.'s may have to wait upon the provision of suitable replacements from volunteers or low-point personnel in Canada (C.A.P.F.) or the United Kingdom.
8.	Therefore non-volunteers now serving with C.A.O.F. and who are non-essential are being
'repatriated as follows:
(a)	All with 110 points and over who can be spared are being returned in Canada drafts during phase three.
That is, following the move of second Canadian infantry division group.
(b)	All with scores between 109 points and 90 points who can be spared are being returned in Canada drafts in phase four.
That is, following the move of third Canadian infantry division group.
(e)^All with scores between 89 points and 50 points who can be spared will be posted to fourth Canadian armoured division before the move of that division and will be repatriated with it.
The succeeding paragraphs deal in rather more detail with some other matters in connection with replacing men now in the occupation force, and one of the main purposes in issuing this second pamphlet was to explain

Demobilization-Army
to the troops in England, in northwest Holland and in the occupation force how that method of replacement would be carried out.

What is to happen to the men who have less than 50 points but did not volunteer to serve in the army of occupation? Are these men to be compelled to stay with the occupation force throughout, even though they have been wounded or have been in action?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thought I indicated that these low-point men are being posted to the occupation force and that provision must be made for replacement of men who are serving in the occupation force. I am'not prepared to say to-day just how long these low-point men may have to serve in that force. They cannot be returned in any event before April or May of next year at the earliest. Before that time arrives, should the occupation commitment continue for some considerable time after that, a plan will be provided for their early replacement, but I am not in a position to state to the committee or to announce what method will be followed or just when these men will be relieved of that duty. That will be announced as soon as possible, but in the meantime the process is going on of replacing relatively high-point men who are now with the occupation force with low-point men, some of whom are in northwest Europe and some of whom are still in the United Kingdom. and who can be released as a result of reducing the holding units of other establishments in the United Kingdom.

Can the minister go so far as to say that it is the intention of the government to replace as quickly as possible all those men who have been in action?
Mr. 'ABBOTT: I will put it in this way. It is the intention of the government to see that the men who are called upon to serve in the occupation force are not required to serve there indefinitely because they happen to be low-point men, whether they have seen action or not. The exact method of replacing them has not yet been determined, or at least I am not in a position to announce how it will be done. I believe, speaking from memory, that an undertaking was given within the last four or five months, or a statement was made, that no man would be required to serve in the occupation force for more than two years. I believe that statement was made.
It is a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I agree that it is a long time, and any plan for replacement, for the working out of which I am responsible, will
contemplate a much shorter term of service than that in the occupation force. I mention that, because my recollection is that the statement was made in the early stages when the occupation force was first being formed.
Will there be .priority for the men who have been in action?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would prefer not to answer that question now without consulting the staff, although I will say this. I see no reason why in the case of the occupation force a distinction should not be made administratively between the man who has seen combat service or action, or something of that kind, and others, in the same way that it was found to be workable in connection with rotation leave, because the numbers involved will be relatively small. The urgency of the shipping problem will not be as great. One of the problems we have now is to be absolutely sure that no space is wasted on any of the transports that are bringing troops back from overseas. We do not wish to take the chance of administrative arrangements falling down and finding ourselves, on the eve of a sailing, with 400 or 500 extra spaces which we cannot fill with men who are entitled to come back at that time. But once the problem is reduced to the size of an occupation force of from twenty to twenty-five thousand, which is the present size, it becomes much more manageable than when we are trying to arrange for the orderly repatriation of a couple of hundred thousand men scattered throughout Europe. I do not wish to be held to this, but it should be quite feasible to provide special priority for the repatriation of men in the occupation force whose points may be low but who have seen some form of combat service. I should think that would be quite feasible.
We are keen that it should be done.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I should think that would
be feasible.

How many potential
replacements has the minister available in England and Canada and northwest Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I asked for that information but I have not the memorandum before me. Certainly, however, I shall have it before the committee rises, and, if not this evening, to-morrow. I have asked for a statement of the up-to-date position of the occupation force. That was sent by airmail from C.M.H.Q., London, on the 26th instant and I would hope to have it to-morrow. There are some variations in the speed of airmail, but I hope to have it to-morrow so that I can give it to the committee.
Demobilization^-Army
Are any men being sent from Canada now as replacements for the occupation force? I refer to men who have not seen action at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think any have been sent as yet but I shall have to verify that with the staff. I believe that consideration is being given to the sending shortly of certain officer personnel, junior officers who have volunteered for the interim force, but there has been no appreciable movement. We have still so many men overseas that we have not felt it was desirable as yet to send additional mouths over to the other side to be fed when we still have from 150,000 to 160,000 men there. I can answer definitely by saying that we have not. There may have been some special men who were sent over but I shall have to verify that. There has been, however, no general movement, and in my judgment there should not be for some months yet because of the large number who of necessity are still there.
Will the men still in Canada be used in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I hope to be able to make an announcement, perhaps before the present session is finished, as to how we plan to provide replacements for the army of occupation, but I am not prepared to make that statement at the moment. Obviously we shall have to provide them from men in Canada.

I do not know if the minister will still answer some of the other questions I asked. I might bring particular ones to his attention now. The first question I asked was, does the minister look upon the N.R.M.A. personnel in Canada as a potential source of recruits for the army of occupation? The second question was, does the press clipping that I spoke of refer to a matter which the minister has under discussion, or is he giving consideration to using the army of occupation as a training ground for the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I had better answer these questions one by one. I shall answer the first question now. Obviously the N.R.M.A. personnel are a potential source of replacement for the army of occupation. Whether they will be used or not is another matter.
As to the press clipping, the press clipping itself has not been used as a basis for discussion; but I will answer my hon. friend by saying that I, as minister, have not considered the occupation force as a potential training ground for our permanent force. I suppose it could be used for that purpose. I have not considered it.

I think I did answer, either in my general statement or specifically, the various points which the hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard raised.
Can the minister give us the N.R.M.A. figures?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes. I promised the hon. member for Vancouver South that I would give the N.R.M.A. figures to-day, if I could get them. I had them this afternoon, but there was no opportunity to give them earlier. I have a report from Canadian military headquarters in London as regards the overseas situation, which says that up to September 30, *1945, 12,927 N.R.M.A. soldiers embarked for overseas. Of those, 950 converted to general service, 67 were killed in action or died of other causes, and 1,217 had returned to Canada up to the end of September, leaving a strength overseas up to that date of 10,693.
The returns from C.M.H.Q. also show that 4,199 of those sent overseas as N.R.M.A. soldiers had proceeded to the continent up to V-E day, and 11,007 had proceeded to the continent up to the end of September. So much for the N.R.M.A. troops overseas. As regards the N.R.M.A. troops in Canada, the strength at October 15 was 23,632, plus 9,575 on extended leave, making a total of 33,207. The break-down of that figure of 23,632 is as follows: in operational units, 1,285; units released to the adjutant general for reallocation, 1,140-
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That means that those units which w'ere operational units are no longer required as such. The men in them have been assigned to the adjutant general for reallocation to other units, for reallocation to depots or wherever it might be. That is the second group. Then, sortation and holding units, 5,651; non-operational units, 10,536.
What would that include?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That includes everything. I believe that has been explained time and again. Some years ago Colonel Ralston said to the staff, "For heaven's sake, try to find another name for them." They have not been able to do that. It includes everything, cooks, staffs in the various depots, those working as ordnance troops on various housekeeping services, and so on, army service corps people, all kinds of people. The operational units, as my hon. friend knows, are coast defence units, and that sort of thing; but these non-operational units cover the field, as it were. The numbers there, as I have said, are 10,536; in the training stream.

225; depot appraisal placement and rehabilitation service, 2,943; employed on administra- ' t-ive and training staffs of reserve army, 52, and in transit 1,800, making up -the total 'of 23,632. As the committee will understand, under present circumstances there is a comparatively large number of troops moving about the country; for as units are disbanded personnel are generally moved to their home districts and employed there, if possible. That accounts for the figure of 1,800- in transit personnel, who on the date of the strength return from which these figures were made up were in transit between port of disembarkation depots in Canada or between various units in Canada. Has the minister the figure of the N.R.M.A. personnel discharged during 1945?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not that figure here but I can obtain it readily. If I do not have it later this evening I will give it to the committee at an early opportunity.
How many of those are of category to be sent overseas?
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not that figure.

Order. I should like to ask hon. members to address the Chair. I am trying to give hon. members who have tried to rise to speak an opportunity to speak. If hon-. members will address the Chair when they rise, as they should, the Chair will try to be fair to everybody.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that it is approximately 15,000, which would include a proportion of those who are on extended leave.

The minister stated a few moments ago that, as far as his information went, no troops had been dispatched overseas to be used in the occupational force since V-E day. I have just this observation to make. There must be a force being built up in Canada to be used- in tlje occupational forces, because I know of several who have volunteered during the past several months to go overseas to act with the occupation troops, and they are now in training.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not anticipate that we shall have any real difficulty in obtaining suitable replacements in Canada to go over
and serve as occupational troops; whether from young troops who joined near the end of the war and who would like to join the army and see the world, or from others who want to sign on with the interim force. But I do not want to make a statement on that now. I want to give the whole question careful consideration with the staff and have a sound plan worked out and ready to put into operation early in the year, which is when it should be started.

When the debate took place yesterday in the committee questions were asked about the method of discharge from the armed forces, and the minister gave some figures as to the number of men returned from overseas. This is what the minister said, as reported on page 1602 of Hansard:	.
In September the reduction in strength from overseas was 35,301, and this is the way in which it worked out. Those with a point score of over 150 were 21,305; those with a point score of 130 to 149-and, mark you, these are all high-point men-were 3,673; those with a point score of 100 to 129 were 3,550; and from 50 to 100 there were only 7,000 out of that total. In other words, well over three-quarters were high-point score men.
I wonder if it would interest the minister and the committee to get the figures with respect to the first divisional group numbering 1,801 men, who arrived back in Toronto a few' weeks ago. The returning group was made up as follows:

The figures given by the minister show that twenty per cent of the men who have been returned to Canada had low-point scores. A great deal was said this afternoon about politics in the army. The other day we had

It is well known in the army that unfortunately many of the senior permanent force officers have always been subject to politics, whether at the hands of the Liberal party or the Conservative party. They are guided by the wishes of whichever party is in power. The minister will realize that when General Simmonds retired Major Macfarlane he did so because Major Macfarlane criticized the manner in which return to Canada was being carried out, and General Simmonds was carrying out the wishes of the minister. To-night the minister stated something about the army of occupation. I am surprised that the minister cannot give the committee the componenl parts of that army as it exists to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I told my hon. friend
that the information was sent from London on the 26th and I will have it to-morrow.

But that army of
occupation has been in existence for a long time, and I am surprised that the minister's department has not the composition of the army at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is changing every day.
In my statement I gave the gross strength of the army.

But I think we are
entitled to the number of units and how the force is made up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is the re-formed third
Canadian division: I gave all that in my initial statement. I was asked in regard to the point score of the men, more or less, and I am getting that information from overseas. The committee can find out quite easily how the force is made up; it has been stated publicly half a dozen times.

The minister said that army was made up of 20,000 men, which is' more than the number of men composing a fighting division. I think he should be able to tell us what units comprise the extra troops. Evidently he is not able to do so. Another thing I believe the minister should tell the committee, what is the purpose of the N.R.M.A. troops to-day? He has told us how they are spread around but he has not told us where these 9,000 deserters are. Are they included in this figure of 38,000.

Well, the people and
especially the men overseas want an answer to the question which was asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. That is, will you use these N.R.M.A. troops as reinforcements? The minister is pretty good at hedging, but I believe the people of this country are entitled to an answer. Obviously the minister does not intend to give one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a matter of government policy which will be announced in due course.

We are here to hear
what the government policy is, and we are asking the minister to tell us. The minister is responsible for his department. He must have some ideas. He must have discussed this matter with his staff, and I think we are entitled to know whether or not he is going to let the men who are overseas to-day get back to this country. I think we should know also what he proposes to do with the N.R.M.A. army if he is not going to use them as reinforcements. They are costing the country a great deal of money, and in my opinion they should be used for that purpose; they should not be demobilized to get the jobs.
Another matter I desire to bring to the attention of the minister is that of the second army university course. The minister must know something about this. Early in 1943, in order to get good officer material, a number of promising young Canadians were taken from various schools and were persuaded to go to university in what was then called the university army course. These young boys completed their year at the university and then were sent to Petawawa and other military camps for advanced training. After they

Demobilization-Army
arrived at these camps, the reinforcement crisis arose and the officers in charge of the various training centres had these young boys paraded. They were made to sign waivers, waiving their right to commissions in the army, with the result that being trained they were immediately sent overseas and they did not spend the time in Canadian camps that was spent by other men in taking basic training. That, of course, was right, because they had done their basic training at the universities. Those young boys were sent to England and through force of circumstances were sent right into the front line in Italy and later in Germany. In the main those boys, when they went into the universities to take this course, were below army age, but they were prepared to accept the duties of citizenship. Now this government, for which the minister must accept some responsibility, has let these men down. I have a letter here from one of these boys from which I think I should read the committee an excerpt:
In June '43 I completed my senior matriculation and immediately enlisted. At the time I was but seventeen. In September '43 I attended successfully No. 2 Canadian army university course for which I received credit in first year engineering at the university of Toronto. I have now been in the army over two years and have served in Italy, Holland and Germany with the first division. In June, because of my comparatively low point score, I was involuntarily put in the occupation force.
With 48 points I am forced to remain in Germany while others with 50 points have already returned home. Many of these men were never in action and many just arrived on the continent in June. Why should a difference of two points mean a waste of one, two or perhaps three years of a man's life?
That is a serious situation. Consideration should be given to those boys; because of their training at universities they receive no credit for points in Canada. As this boy says, he has 48 points, and is in the army of occupation against his wishes. Had he got points for the year at university in Canada he would have had 72 points in all and might be on his way home now. I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to those boys who left school and went to an army university course, and who cannot get home at this time.
A great deal has been said to-day about brass hats. I do not attack the brass hats as brass hats. If we are to have an army worth while in Canada we should not ridicule them all the time, because if we do we will make it impossible for the right calibre of men to join the services. The minister has given his sincere assurance that where there is inefficiency he will wipe it out. I am satis-47696-105
fied that if we want to - make the services attractive to the young men of to-day we must stop sniping at them.	.

I have just a word to say about brass hats. I shall describe the reception received by General Crerar, Canada's greatest soldier, in my home town of Riviere du Loup. Let me say at the outset that when a reception is organized by the local authorities, including the municipal council and local citizens, everything is fine. In that small town of 9,000 people there was a complete organization to give to Their Majesties the King and Queen the finest reception they received in the province of Quebec. It was the last reception in that province and, as a result of the sincerity of the reception, the queen was moved to tears before she left. The organization was well arranged so that all had an opportunity to see Their Majesties. They talked with everyone and the people were satisfied. The children sang, and Their Majesties were delighted with the reception.
Then, when General Crerar returned from his glorious campaign in Europe a large crowd of people gathered to see him at the station of Riviere du Loup. The place for the reception should have been behind the station, where there is' a large area of ground, and thousands of people could have seen him and applauded. Instead of that, however, the whole thing was under the military authorities of Quebec city, headed by Brigadier Edmond Blais of M.D. No. 5. Instead of putting the stand behind the station where it would have accommodated the crowd of thousands of people, not expecting so many people to come he put the stand between the train and the baggage shed. In addition to that, a fence was erected to keep the people from seeing' the general-just the same as if they had been cattle. We know how cattle are fenced in, in station yards.
That fence was an insult to the people. The place set aside for the reception was surrounded by all the brass hats from Ottawa. It was only large enough for them and, with the exception of a few select citizens, no others could see him. An invitation was extended to the mayor, the municipal councillors and a few other people, among whom I was fortunate to be included. Upon arriving there I found the reception had been strangely organized.
The general spoke first; then the brigadier invited his worship the mayor to extend a welcome, after the general had spoken- something I found quite extraordinary. In addition to that, the loud speaker for the radio was not properly installed and did not

Demobiliza lion-Army

work well, with the result that no one could hear anything and, in addition, as I have already pointed out, with the exception of a few, the people had not been invited. The veteran's guard were not there. Who were there? It was the band of the 22nd battalion-without instruments. With two or three exceptions, those veterans who were passed in review were not people of that place-; they were the musicians who were there and who at great expense had been brought from Quebec. It was an insult to the veterans of Riviere du Loup, and also an insult to the parents of the soldiers and returned men. The citizens, on instructions of the brigadier, were kept by the police outside the sight of the general.
That is the way in which th^ reception was organized. As I have said, the band of the 22nd battalion was there, but without instruments. When the general left it was not the band that played God Save The King. They just put a broken record on a gramophone, and that was all that was played when the general left.
But it was worse than that. The brigadier was gracious enough to take upon himself the duty of introducing everyone to General Crerar, and he had to talk to everyone before making an introduction. "You are Mr.-?" "Mr. So-and-so". "Mr. So-and-so; General Crerar." "You are Mr.-?" "Mr. This and That". "Mr. This and That; General Crerar". The introductions were made like that. It was an insult to the people of Riviere du Loup. That is the kind of brass hats we have.
I will mention to the hon. member for York South another stupidity of the brass hats in Ottawa. I took upon myself the responsibility of recommending Colonel Triquet for promotion. What was the answer I got from those swivel-chair heroes who won the war from Ottawa? It was that Colonel Triquet was not ready at that time for promotion to officer rank. They are there, and when I speak they beat their brows and are very indignant.
There must be some reform. No reform was made by the two previous ministers of national defence. From the death of the late Norman Rogers to the time the present minister was appointed there was a gap at the head of the Department of National Defence. Both ministers were alike, and consequently they made no reforms. I was even called to order because I called the brass hats pompous. It was the greatest humiliation of my life when I could not proceed any farther without withdrawing the word "pompous". The record is there.
I will ask the Minister of National Defence if his job is not a full-time one. We had as one of his predecessors in the Department of

National Defence a man who was an amateur minister of national defence and whose main business was that of acting minister of finance. He was concocting schemes with Allan Magee and with Harry Borden and other big-wigs of the same category. They were always concocting things, schemes for the post-war period. I turn my thumbs down on them once more. It was a scandal from beginning to end. I remember what was said in this house during the fall session when conscription was decided upon.
We were being told everywhere that one should be discreet; that one should be careful; that one should watch his words, because any indiscretion might cause the death of thousands of men.. Mum was the word. Be silent. Be careful. Watch your step. Do not say anything that could be used by the enemy. These warnings were posted in all cars. We saw the head of a man who was drowning because of an indiscretion that had been committed by some one with too long a tongue.
But there was something worse than all that, and this happened in the house. There was that stupid, criminal discussion about the need of reinforcements on the front. Who was it said that? One of the former ministers of national defence and some hon. members on the other side were telling the whole world that the allied forces were too weak to resist the enemy. That is what was said in this very chamber. I was scandalized, because I could not believe that men with heads on their shoulders would speak like that and give such information to the enemy, whether it was true or not. We should have been sitting in camera; that was not a matter to be aired, in the House of Commons of Canada. It was taken up by the press and by the radio, and the whole world was informed that a former minister of national defence, a man who was considered to be more important by those who did not know him than he really was, a man with some, importance because of his high functions, was saying that there was a weak spot in the allied forces on the European continent.
What happened? A short time after the special session when that nonsensical talk had taken place we had an offensive by von Runstedit when 60,000 allied men were made prisoners of war. Everyone who thinks about it must be sure that that was brought about by the silly talk of the former minister of national defence and some members of the opposition during that special session. It was an inducement to the Germans to play their last.card and try to break the allied lines on the continent of Europe. That is what happened. I consider that those men used criminal

Demobilization-Army
language, language that cost the lives of thousands of people. I denounce that with all the strength that I can use.
Not only that; I ask the hon. member from York South to consider what the former minister of national defence did when he was asked by the allied command to send some of our best grade men to Italy when they were not required. They were sent there to suffer misery and death. I can speak of this because many boys from my county met death and torture in Sicily and Italy. That was decided by the brass hats. Why? Because they wanted to have conscription as a political issue. They were playing politics here in Ottawa. What was the trouble? It was these people who could think only of politics. They were thinking, not of winning the war but of winning political battles, and they were ready to use conscription as a political issue. They have used a sword which is covered with blood, not their own blood but the blood of others. They attempted to rouse the Canadian people and make a political issue out of it.
If the hon. member for York South is sincere in saying that he wants to cut expenses, I refer him to the Woods building and all these other buildings where the brass hats of the army, navy and air are to be found.

This afternoon one or two speeches were made dealing with what the speakers felt was discrimination in connection with promotions in the armed services. If any hon. member wishes to check back, I refer him to page 595 of Hansard where answers are given to some questions that were asked. It would appear that at that time not only was there some discrimination in connection with the matter brought up this afternoon by hon. members across the floor or the suggestion that there was discrimination because of political affiliations or belief, but there was also some discrimination based upon geography or the location of the particular depots.
I checked over these figures, and I found that the ratio of promotions of commissioned ranks to other ranks varied considerably. I found that Pacific command, which is Victoria, showed a ratio of 1 to 11 -7. I thought, with that area being near salt water and the men probably eating a lot of fish, they might have more brains than the men on the prairies. However, when I got down to M.D. No. 3, where there is no salt water, I found the ratio to be 1 to 9-2. Then, when we come to Montreal, M.D. No. 4, we find the ratio is 1 to 9-7. We can work west to Winnipeg where we find that the ratio is 1 to 14-5. We go farther west to Regina and find that the ratio is 1 to 17-4.
It looks to me that the minister has something to explain there, and obviously he will have some kind of explanation to give. But with these figures it will be difficult to explain to the people on the prairies just why they do not have the same ratio of promotions as the other provinces. For the sake of making this available to those members who may be interested and to people outside, I should like to read into the record some figures showing the way in which this works out.
Starting with 'London, which is M.D. No. 1, we find that the total of general service enlisted personnel-this has nothing to do with the N.R.M.A.-all ranks, was 48,250. Of that number, 3,099 were officers and 45,151 other ranks. The ratio there is 1 to 14-5.
In the case of Toronto, M.D. No. 2, the total of general service personnel, all ranks, was 145,583. The total officers were 10,379, and the total of other ranks, 135,204. The ratio in this case wa4 1 to 13.
In the case of Kingston, M.D. No. 3, which comprises the area of Ottawa, where the hon. member for Temiscouata has just told us there are so many brass hats, the total for all ranks was given as 55,495. There were 5,392 officers and 50,103 other ranks, giving a ratio of 1 to 9'2.
In Montreal, M.D. No. 4, the total for all ranks was 72.597. The total for officers was 6,739 and for other ranks, 65,858, giving a ratio of 1 to 9-7.
Quebec, M.D. No. 5: total all ranks, 22,183; total officers, 1,844; total other ranks, 20,339, or a ratio of 1 to 11.
Halifax, M.D. No. 6 and this belies the idea that fish make brains, because all these figures approximate to those of Regina, which is irf the prairie provinces-total, all ranks, 49,487; officers, 2,278; total other ranks, 46,709, or a ratio of 1 to 16-8.
Saint John, M.D. No. 7: total all ranks, 32,268; total officers, 1,912; total other ranks, 30,356, or a ratio of 1 to 15-8. Fish do not do them much good.
Winnipeg, M.D. No. 10: total all ranks, 54,061; total officers, 3,478; total other ranks, 50,583, or a ratio of 1 to 14-5.
Victoria, M.D. No. 11 (Pacific command): total all ranks, 54,746; total officers, 4,291; total other ranks, 50,455, or a ratio of 1 to 11-7.
Regina, M.D. No. 12: total all ranks, 44,684; total officers, 2,426; total other ranks, 42,258, or a ratio of 1 to 17-4.
Calgary, M.D. No. 13: total all ranks, 46,919; total officers, 2,737; total other ranks, 44,182, or a ratio of 1 to 16-1., As they get nearer British Columbia the intelligence quotient apparently goes up.

We also have some from outside Canada. As I say, there was talk this afternoon of discrimination in respect of the language question. Whether it is well founded or not I do not know. There, was talk of discrimination because of political beliefs; that was denied by the Minister of Agriculture. No doubt some reason will be shown for this condition I have mentioned, but it will be difficult, unless the reason is good, to explain to the people of the prairie provinces why they do not have the same ratio of promotions as in M.D. No. 3 around Ottawa, and in Quebec and Victoria.

To begin with. I should like to associate myself with what has been said so well by the hon. members for Vancouver South, Nanaimo, Vancouver-Burrard and Kamloops during this debate, particularly in regard to the point system of demobilization and repatriation of our men overseas and the revision of that system as suggested by some of these speakers.
May I refer for a moment to a case which .happened in my own riding, the particularly distressing case of a family who gave five sons-all they had-to serve in this war. All these sons have been overseas for periods of over two years, and one of them was killed on active service. The father became seriously ill a, few weeks ago, and the request was made to have at least two of these sons returned home on compassionate grounds. I may say here that the minister * has done everything he could to see that this was complied with, and I do not blame him in any way for the fact that these sons did not arrive home before the father passed away ten days ago. I do not know what the routine is; but under the circumstances put before the minister two or three weeks ago, and on which he took immediate action, some officer overseas failed to see the urgency, and although the funeral was held up for several days, none of these boys arrived home, nor have arrangements yet been made to permit them to return to Canada. I am mentioning this case to show, in the first place, the great contribution which this family has made to the winning of the war and, second, the tardiness shown by some officers in carrying out their

duties. I doubt whether any other family in Canada has had a better record than the one which I have just mentioned.
I desire for a moment to refer to the subject of scientific research, which has such an important place in the defence services, particularly as related to national defence policy.
There are three broad fields in which Canadians are at present interested and in which I believe Canada can make an effective contribution in research and perhaps in development : first, the electronic field-radar, radio communication, and so forth; second, the atomic energy project now in operation under the national research council; third, jet propulsion in all its aspects. I should like to ask the government through the Minister of National Defence if they have made any plans with regard to these highly important developments, and, if so, what those plans are.
A study of the National Research Act will disclose the fact that the work which the national research council was expected to do under this act has never been carried out. The council is first of all an administrative body, and its secondary function is to operate its own laboratories.
What is the government going to do to coordinate national defence technical requirements with the three services? It should be obvious to anyone that in so far as research is concerned these services should be brought together in peace time and put under the control and direction of the national research council.
With its vast war-time production, Research Enterprises developed all the technical skill which is necessary to make almost anything, and it would be nothing short of a national calamity if this technical knowledge and skill were lost to the country. There are so many things to which it could be turned. For example, it would enable us to make surgical and precision instruments and optical equipment now imported from Germany, England or the United States. If this plant is scrapped, what will the government do for optical glass? What will it do for optics? What are the government's plans in connection with TurboResearch? May I emphasize the necessity of placing all this research under a central organization. We are fortunate in having such an organization which has been functioning efficiently for years, namely, the national research council, ready to assume this responsibility. I wish to pay the highest tribute to the initiative, vision and organizing ability of those men in charge of Research Enterprises, who starting from scratch, selected and trained young men and women in entirely new fields,

Demobilization-Army
and in an incredibly short time turned out by mass production over $200 million worth of precision instruments and radar equipment-which played such an important part in winning this war.
I understand that in all their work they have been closely associated with the national research council. I call attention to the fact that in doing this work the company has developed a large body of individuals with specialized skill and with practical knowledge of the methods employed in the manufacture of the above-mentioned articles, which should not be lost to the country.
May I urge the government to initiate, under their direction, a continuing field of opportunity for these individuals, so that it may be possible to retain their technical skill. It is possible that enough optical instruments will not be required to make it profitable for private enterprise, but from the point of view of its national importance this scientific skill should- be retained.
The German government, realizing the national importance of the optical industry, supported the well known firm of Zeiss for a period of years in creating and maintaining the largest optical munitions source in the world. Without government assistance this firm could never have developed to the extent that it did. Incidentally I might mention that, apparently, Russia has taken over this entire plant and will probably transfer it to its own country. Can we afford to be dependent on a foreign country for our optical instruments, which play such a big part in war? It should not be necessary to urge the government to maintain a small part of Research Enterprises where this industry may be continued under government direction and control, perhaps through the national research council, and where the employment of a small group of trained personnel may be retained.
Research Enterprises could make a contribution to the plan of post-war arsenals, whatever that plan may be, by the facilities which it can offer as well as by providing the skilled personnel to whom I have just referred, and I suggest that this could be done through a government-owned company. I understand that Turbo-Research Limited has been and presumably will be operated within the framework of Research Enterprises and should be developed, not because of any commercial possibilities, but as a necessary policy of defence. If this Turbo-Research were to continue in the way suggested it would be able to make use of a variety of services and production facilities of Research Enterprises. The residual facilities of Research Enterprises, including personnel, could be utilized under this plan.
Of course, it \yill be obvious that the continuing plan will be greatly reduced, but even so it will give an opportunity of keeping alive highly trained technical personnel and equipment in a degree of readiness to meet any emergency. Through Turbo-Research or in some other way, residual groups of trained personnel could be maintained in the instrument and radio divisions and be immediately available. In other words, I suggest that some of the buildings now occupied by Research Enterprises eould be retained and have productive facilities in a state of readiness, with a nucleus of trained personnel whose potential skills could be utilized on projects arising in connection with defence services technical requirements.
The research work now carried on in the army signals establishment in Ottawa and in the naval signal school at St. Hyacinthe could be transferred to this unit at Research Enterprises under the direction of the national research council. There is a large field of fire control which eould also be included in the same unit, but perhaps the most important work would be in the field of radar and telecommunications.
Surely one does not have to labour the argument in making out the strongest possible case for the retention and development of such scientific work by the federal government in the building under its own control, upon which a very large amount of the taxpayers' money has already been spent, with skilled technicians who, if allowed to disperse, would inevitably be lost to the country.
May I refer to opportunities in the radar field. The national research council at Ottawa had responsibility for research and design in radar. In view of the fact that two fields at Unionville and Scarboro were used in connection with facilities at Leaside, might it not be well to consider the physical removal to the latter place of design functions formerly carried on in the city of Ottawa.
In connection with radar development I should like to refer to cathode ray tubes. I understand that a variety of types of these articles were produced in quantities at Research Enterprises. It would seem to be highly desirable to maintain this establishment, since the retention under government control of this cathode ray tube facility may be of national importance.
I think everyone will realize that the production of weapons and equipment for modern war will depend upon the permanent development of technical facilities and skills in every nation. If we are to play our part in future defence, then we must develop in Canada sufficient technical skill in this field, with neces-
