Demobilization-Army

sary scientific personnel and facilities. With such a central plan provision would be made for a common meeting place for each of the three services with scientific design and development personnel, and an industry sufficient for the purposes to make us independent of any foreign country. I suggest, therefore, that the national research council is the body in Canada which should provide such a national organization. We have available in Canada to-day scientific personnel, trained workers and laboratory and production facilities needed for such a plan by any national defence policy which is put into effect.
I know that the tendency has been for each of the services to create and maintain its own technical establishment in the field of design and development, but I submit that it would effect a great economy, as well as increase of efficiency, if these were combined. May I therefore suggest that the government create a committee or body with the president of the national research council as its chairman and that membership be provided for representatives of the government, as well as of the three national defence services, which would correlate and direct the scientific development and technical requirements of each of the defence services, which, of course, includes the medical branches. There will, no doubt, be great progress made in the years to come, in developments that will follow technical investigations, and it is, therefore, vitally important that we should have ' a central coordinating organization such as this, so that the scientific and technical requirements of the three defence services may be dealt with by one central body.
May I again repeat that the national research council is the logical central body through which the requirements of all our defence services should be coordinated and directed.
In order to give force and meaning to the suggestions which I have made, I should like to refer briefly to one outstanding example of a valuable contribution made by Research Enterprises to our allies during the war. When the United States entered the war, that country was not producing radar, and Research Enterprises supplied within two months four complete radar equipments for the protection of the Panama canal, so vital to shipping. I understand that, later on, large quantities of a type of light mobile radar equipment w;as supplied exclusively by Research Enterprises and played a very important part in the landing operations in the early stages of the Pacific war.
May I call the minister's attention for a moment to the medical sendees and make a

suggestion in connection therewith? During the war I have not criticized the fact that we have had three separate anti distinct medical services, one for the navy, one for the army and one for the air force. I have felt that this duplication or triplication was perhaps justified by the distinctive character of the problems which each had to face. Now that the war is over, however, in my opinion there is no longer justification for the large additional expenditures which will be involved in -triplicating medical services, especially since this will not improve the medical care of our men but may have the opposite effect, as I will show in a moment.
After all, the treatment remains the same whether the sickness occurred or the wounds were received in service in the army, navy or air force. It will avoid much confusion and expense and promote a higher degree of efficiency if all highly trained specialists are available for the three services under one supreme head. Therefore I suggest that there should be one director general of medical services with three deputies, one each for the navy, army and air force. I suggest further that under these arrangements medical officers and nurses who have served in the navy, army or air force should be given the right to wear their distinctive uniforms.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There are four questions which I should like to put to the minister. I imagine I had better do so now, because under the special items I do not see places where I may ask them.
Before I address my questions to the minister may I say that I listened with interest to the last speaker in connection with the two matters which he discussed before the committee. I believe that consideration should be given to his latter contention, namely, combining the medical services of the various armed forces. I also wish to congratulate him on making the appeal that he did for increasing the part that the government should play in research. I suggest that it might be put on an even broader basis than just an interest in defence, important as that may be. I certainly hope that when the proper item comes before the house, namely the estimates of the national research council, we may be able to get the admission of the government that definite increases have to be made in our expenditures for research. I shall have something more to say about that when the item comes up; it is hardly under discussion at the present time.
The first question I should like to ask is whether further consideration has been given, and whether anything has come out of that

Demobilization-Army
consideration, to the request that stepmothers be awarded the Silver Cross which is awarded to mothers of men who have given their lives. The minister knows that this matter has been raised before. It does not affect a great many people, but seems a little strange that the line should be drawn so hard in this particular case. I need only mention the fact that there are cases of stepmothers who have fdled that place from the infancy of the soldier who has now given his life. The government should find a way to relent on its previous stand and make that award without further delay.
The second question I should like to put to the minister has to do with the awarding of the 1939-45 medal and also the Pacific star to the men who went to Hong Kong. In my own city of Winnipeg there is at the present time a great deal of rejoicing as these men are coming home. And when one thinks of the fact that these awards were to be given for service in the Pacific surely they should be given to these men. I would go further, as has_ already been suggested in this house by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and suggest that all of the special allowances that were to have been made for fighting in the Pacific should be accorded those men who went to Hong Kong in 1941, retroactive to the time they left Canada.
I move on to the third question that I should like to put to the minister. It relates to the men of the brigade which went to Kiska, This question, like the previous one, has been up in the house before. These men went on an expedition that might have cost heavily in terms of casualties. Even so, there were some casualties owing to mines and so on which were left behind by the enemy, which, without the knowledge of our forces, had fled. I remind the minister that these men were overseas. They endured pretty difficult conditions for a period of about six months. They were in an area which was recognized in connection with the United States troops with whom they were serving as a combat zone, and it does seem to me that the request of the men and their officers should be considered and they should be awarded at least the 1939-45 star. I do not want to raise any of the invidious comparisons that are sometimes made in this committee, but I do hope this award is not being withheld because a large number of the troops in that brigade were N.R.M.A. men. The fact is that they were sent on the expedition. After repeated representation it was recognized as overseas by the income tax department ; it was on the other side of the 180th
meridian, and it does seem to me this award should be made to these men. I know they feel very keenly about it and are not satisfied with the way in which their request for consideration of this matter has been put off from time to time.
There is a fourth matter about which I should like to question the minister, and I shall do so by referring to a specific case which I mention because I am interested in the soldier I have in mind and also because I believe that a principle is at stake, since indeed there must be a great many others in a similar situation. I do not wish to mention the name of this soldier, for reasons which will be obvious in a moment, but to make it clear that I am talking about a specific case I will give his number, which is H-9501. This young man enlisted in the army while still very young; he was sent to England in due course and was most anxious to play his part to the full. He is the son of a veteran of the last war, and it was in his very blood to make the best contribution he could in this war for the defence of his country. He did everything he could to get to Italy as soon as possible after reaching England, and managed to get included in a volunteer draft after being in England- for only three months.
In Italy in September, 1941, this young man, who was a private, was in the very thick of the fighting. He was in the battle of the Gothic line, and up front at least three times. I have talked to him myself, and the simplest way for me to put it is to say that he went through hell itself in his experiences at the Gothic line. He took part in bayonet charges; as hon. members who have been through this sort of thing will appreciate, much of the time he was crawling on his stomach, facing all the horrors and hazards of front-line warfare at its worst. I mention with emphasis the fact that he was only twenty years of age, and I suggest to the minister that many men of his age and younger went through a terrible experience. The plain fact of the matter is that the time came when the strain became too great; he cracked up and left the front line. Within three hours he gave himself up and was anxious to make up for what he had done, to go back to the front line. The fellow soldiers to whom he gave himself up saw the condition he was in and felt it was useless for him to go back to the front line. Rightly or wrongly, they assisted him to get farther back, and suggested that he give himself up farther behind the lines. By the time he did so, of course he was absent without leave and in due course was court martialed and given a sentence of two years detention.
Demobilization-Army

I took up this case on a number of occasions with the minister's predecessor. I was assured that it would be investigated, but that was about all that ever happened until shortly after the present minister came into office. Very soon after that, I am glad to say, the case of this soldier was reviewed at least to the extent that his release from detention was ordered. In the meantime he had been brought home from Italy to Canada, and endured the experience of being handcuffed while in public in a place like Toronto. Later he was taken to Kingston, from where he was released a short while ago. Now, of course, he stands discharged from the army, and his discharge certificate reads "for misconduct", so that he loses his gratuities and all that sort of thing. Beyond that, however, this young man will have to go through life under a stigma, whereas the fact of the matter is that he did his best to make the fullest possible contribution and, if I might go back to the expression I used a moment ago, he went through hell itself for the sake of his country.
I fully realize the need for discipline, especially when the battle is on, or I might even go farther and say, while the war is still on. It does seem to me in this case, however-and I quote it because according to my information there are many like it-that the sentence has been far too severe, and I would earnestly hope that this case might be reviewed with the thought that a change might be made in the basis of this young man's discharge. He knows the seriousness of what he did; he knew within three hours how serious it was, even under the strain he was experiencing. But he paid the price for all that in the severity of the punishment which was imposed upon him; in the sentence he was given and in the way he served that sentence, and it does seem to me that should be enough. I suppose some of the military people would say I am calling for a complete overhaul of policy in these matters. Well, all .right; I call for it. It seems to me that in this citizen army about which we have had so much to say to-day we should be human in matters like these. I was pleased that the young man in question was released shortly after the present minister came into office. I can tell him that the family of this young man give him the credit. Whether or not the minister should get it, at least he is being given credit for the release of this soldier.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I had nothing to do with it. I should like to take credit for it, but I cannot.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Then I will give the minister an opportunity now to get credit for

something else if he will have this case reviewed still further. I have presented the matter to him by correspondence, and two or three weeks ago by letter he did assure me that he would have the matter looked into, get a full report on it and get in touch with me again when he had that report. But I urge that, even if it involves some drastic change in policy, the minister see if we cannot do something so that young men like this, who have made such a real contribution to the defence of this country, will not go through life under the sort of stigma this young man is experiencing at the present time. I know the family; I know the young man himself. They happen to live in my constituency. That is why I speak of the case as one I know something about. I come to the minister now with an appeal for his most sympathetic consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This, of course, is one of many similar cases. These questions concerning the sentences of courts martial are coming up for review all the time. The circumstances as my hon. friend has outlined them certainly would arouse one's sympathy. When he began to talk of this case I thought it was another, very similar case which occurred in Italy, where a man left the front line under fire and was found in the wagon lines next morning. It was one of those cases where the man took this action under heavy stress, and he was sentenced by court martial. All these cases are being reviewed in the ordinary way, and, I think, are being reviewed sympathetically. When any case of that kind is brought, not necessarily to the attention of myself but to the attention of the secretary of the department, a sympathetic investigation will be held. I know the veterans affairs committee is now discussing the question of a review of the grounds of discharge of various members of the armed forces, perhaps more from the point of view of how a man's gratuity is affected. All I can say is that there is a procedure laid down under the Army Act for appeals from sentences to the minister and to the governor in council, and a good many of those come forward. From my brief, but fairly active experience, I know that all of them receive careful consideration. I am sure they received careful consideration from my predecessors, and the ones which come before me are looked into carefully. I do not recall the particular case my hon. friend has in mind, but I have taken a note of the number, and I recall'mention of a review of this case. I think it is now under way.
The other three questions have been brought up before. First, there is the question of granting the Memorial Cross to stepmothers. That was the subject of an answer given a

Demobilization-Army
week or two ago. So far as I know there has been no further consideration of the matter since that time. I shall bring my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the committee, which has considered this matter time and again to see if there is anything which might lead them to change their opinions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What are the objections?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Broadly speaking, it was that this should be restricted to blood relations, such as mothers and wives. It has never been extended to stepmothers. It was felt that if it were extended to stepmothers it should perhaps logically be extended to other relatives, such as sisters and the like. Whether those grounds are sufficient or not, I cannot say. In any event it has received much careful consideration over a considerable period of time, and that was the decision taken. It has been brought up before. All I can say is that I shall look into it again to see if I think there is any real ground for extending it to others than those already eligible.
Then, as to the Pacific Star, I believe I answered a question in the house when the matter was first raised some weeks ago. I pointed out that the eligibility for this star, with others, was fixed by regulations which were common to all the commonwealth nations, but I felt sure that the Pacific Star would be awarded, and that those who served in Hong Kong would be eligible for that star. I cannot make a positive statement to-night, but my former statement will stand. They will get the star.
I do not know about the 1939-45 medal. I shall have to look into that. I am inclined to think they are eligible, but I shall have to make my answer later.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What about the 1939-45 star for the Kiska men?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to look into that, too.
Don't waste your time.
I think too much of the hon. member for Fraser Valley to give him the answer he should get.
What is that?
I think too much of the hon. member for Fraser Valley to give him the answer he should get for making that interjection when I rose to speak.
Pardon me; I was not referring to the hon. member. I was referring to the ridiculous remark about Kiska.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is your opinion.

I thank the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I was sure he did not mean any offence; I just wished to give him a bit of a bouquet, because he deserves one now and again.
If the question I am about to ask has been answered before, I shall not expect the minister to answer it. If not, then I am sure he will forgive me for asking it. What is to be done for the fire-fighters who went overseas under the command of Fire Chief Gordon Huff of Brantford? What is being done, and by what department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They were under the jurisdiction of my colleague the Minister of National War Services. He has-or had-them under his wing.

I rise with some diffidence at this late hour, because so many distinguished soldiers and officers of this war and the last one have already spoken. Because of the small part I played in the first war, perhaps the committee would excuse me if I were to make some suggestions to the minister.
First of all, I was interested in the officer mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I was interested in the fact that apparently there was a forum in the army. I knew that something like that was going on in England at the beginning of the war, because I remember quite well that during the lull which occurred immediately after the outbreak of war the question was often asked as to who commanded a battalion, a private or the colonel. Apparently it was resolved in favour of the colonel at that time-I suppose by process of alternative voting.
I was not so sure when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was speaking that a man who might be a good speaker in one of those forums might make a good officer. Some people would think that if he were a good talker he might make a worse officer than someone else who did less talking. After all, there is great opportunity for men in the ranks.
While in the last war the subalterns took credit for being the brains and back-bone of the army, I am told that in this one it is the sergeants who claim that they won the war. I had noticed before the speech of the hon, member for Melfort that there was a considerable number of officers in proportion to the number of enlistments. There were 45,000 commissioned ranks out of a total enlistment of 730,000 which, I believe, included some in the women's organizations. At the beginning of this war we were told that there were only

Demobilization-Army

to be three officers per company in the infantry, and when I remember that I can not see where this large number of officers could be used. I realize, of course, that the dental, medical and chaplain corps would have a considerable number of officers. But even including them I could not see where in this war we required so many officers.
The minister also spoke about the great work done in connection with enlistments in this war, and compared those enlistments with those of the last war. It seemed to me that he put the enlistments of the last war in a somewhat unfavourable light. I find that, according to his own statement, there were enlistments in the army in this war numbering
730.000.	of whom only 370,000 went overseas. He pointed out that the casualties amounted to 80,000. I may be wrong, but I believe that figure included casualties in all the forces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Just the army.

All hon. members know that the air force suffered a considerable number of casualties. My memory is that in the last war enlistments in the armed forces of Canada totalled about 650,000, of whom
465.000	went overseas. That is, 465,000 out of
650.000	in the first war, as compared with
370.000	out of 730,000 in this war.
In the last war we know that the fatal casualties numbered nearly 60,000, and the minister has said that all casualties numbered
200.000.	My recollection was that the fatalities were much higher, and, if the minister's figures are correct, then one-third of all the casualties were fatal. My recollection was that the total wounded ran to something over
300.000.	So that I do not think the government has any reason to congratulate itself when it compares what it has done in this war with what was done in the last one.
I have heard a great deal said at different times-and much was said during the last parliament-to the effect that universal service in the last war did not produce men in the front lines, that the results were negligible so far as reinforcements were concerned.
I recall about a year ago, or in the spring, I have forgotten which, I was in my own home when the present Prime'Minister spoke over the radio and made that statement. The actual figures show that after universal service was brought into effect, 157,000 joined up, voluntarily or otherwise, of whom a considerable number went overseas. While the speech was being made over the radio, I became rather worked up, and I immediately stopped listening to the Prime Minister and got out my old A company book of the third- battalion. I found that in my company sixty
	.
men had numbers of 2,000,000 or over, which, as I understood it, showed they had joined after the introduction of compulsory service. That was on the day hostilities ceased, November 11, 1918. They comprised practically half of my old company. A considerable number of these men had acquitted- themselves very honourably and favourably in the preceding battle. Many had been either killed or wounded. If another battle had taken place it would have been fought largely by men who had joined up, either compulsorily or otherwise, after universal service had been brought into force.
The conscripted men who went overseas in th^ last war were not tagged, but unfortunately they were given a number which gave away the fact that they had been conscripted. But they never were treated any differently from the other men. I know that many of these men- were rather glad that someone else had made up their minds for them. Many of them had held back for family or other reasons. They did not feel they ought to take the plunge and join the army and they were glad when that was decided for them.
We all know the trouble that occurred during this war in connection with the reinforcement situation in the front line. I do not 'know whether I should blame the minister because I do not think he was in charge, but perhaps I shall have to blame the government because they must take the responsibility for what is done by the officers who look after military matters. As I passed up and down the country, by train or otherwise, I met many of the boys in the armed forces. I asked them what branch of the service they belonged to, and I found out they would be in the ordnance, in mechanical transport, in the R.C.E.M.E. and other -branches; seldom did I meet an infantry man. I take no credit for saying at that time, "You may -be in the ordnance to-day but you will be somewhere else to-morrow because heavy casualties are always suffered by the infantry."
I cannot see why those in charge of the government did not foresee that casualties due to the present terrible engines of war would- soon -wipe out the number of men they had allocated to the infantry. We have heard the hon. member for Calgary East tell us what happened to his battery, how it was converted into infantry. I have -heard of other instances where that -was done-.
If a man has done nothing but remain overseas for several years, in my opinion he should receive a considerable number of points more than the man who has been in Canada. Even though a man has -been located in British Columbia he will have had opportunity to

Demobilization-Army
visit his folks quite frequently. Certainly the man actively engaged in fighting in the front line should receive a considerable number of points in addition to those received by other men overseas.
It does seem too bad if men who have been in the front line and who have suffered the terrible strain of front-line warfare should, be kept in the occupation forces when there are others available. The minister has given figures to-night showing that there are about 11,000 N.R.M.A. men in England or in Europe. Certainly I would expect that those men would be used in their entirety. I cannot see how the government can justify holding 35,000 N.R.M.A. men in Canada without sending them overseas if they are required. The government should release some of these men who have been through these battles; they should release some of the other long service men. The reinforcements would be facing no danger; they would be taking what we used to call in the last war a Cook's tour. Sufficient of these' men should be sent over to take the place of those who are entitled to come home.
This evening the minister spoke of training key men for the occupation force. Six months have elapsed since V-E day in May and I wonder why men have not been trained to take the place of those who are supposed to be key men. I know that officers in charge like to retain men who are efficient, but after all that cannot always be done even in business. I submit that there are a great many men who are supposed to be key men who could be sent home, even though this might cause some little inconvenience to the officers in charge. The minister referred to a pamphlet which is dated September 6, 1945, less than two months ago and I notice that this statement is made:
C.A.O.F. is setting up its own trades schools to train low-score men or volunteers to replace non-volunteer tradesmen and specialists.
It seems to me that the minister might quite properly be dissatisfied with an overseas headquarters which has failed in four months to do the obvious thing and give instructions to low-point men in order that they might take the place of those who are now considered essential.

I have only two matters which I desire to raise with the minister. One has to do with the rations which are now supplied to Canadians in the army of occupation in Europe. My question is based upon a complaint which I received in a letter from overseas just this afternoon. I should like to ask whether the rations given to the army of occupation have been reduced in any way, either as to quality or quantity, as compared 47696-1061
with what was supplied to the troops under similar circumstances while hostilities were on. The minister might indicate to the committee just what reduction has taken place and the reasons therefor.	,

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not know the exact date, but either last week or ten days ago the ration scale in the army of occupation was varied or reduced. For reasons which I think the committee will appreciate, our ration scale has always been the same as the British ration scale. We supplement it with some fruit juices, but by and large our basic ration overseas is the same as the British ration. We draw our rations from the British; the pipeline is the same; the source of supply is the same. Our ration has always conformed to the British ration.
While the troops were engaged in active operations and training on the continent, the ration was somewhat larger than the ration in Great Britain-both British and Canadian troops enjoyed that higher ration scale-there was some more meat and so on. I have not before me the details of the ration, but that is the position. About a week or ten days ago, or it may be as much as two weeks ago, the British ration scale was reduced by eliminating that extra ration for the troops on the continent. In other words, it was felt that by and large conditions of service on the continent were not greatly different from those in England, that the troops were not then engaged in fighting operations, or marching, or the more strenuous operations, and that the scale on the continent should be made to conform to that in Great Britain; and it was felt that so far as our own troops were concerned we must follow the same practice we had done in the past, and that our ration scale would conform to theirs. I can get some further detail as to the way in which it was reduced, but I imagine that is the information which the committee would wish to have.
There has also been a change in the ration scale in Great Britain, as to which I have not yet full particulars, but which I have asked for and will give the committee as soon as I can.
Is it still higher in the arm)' than it is so far as the civilian population in Britain is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I think so-substantially higher; and, of course, very much higher than that of the people in the countries which our troops are occupying.

There is one other matter about which I should like to ask the minister. Is there any form of censorship or scrutiny of the mails by anyone in the army,
Demobilization-Army

in so far as mail coming from the ordinary
private or non-commissioned officer in the army of occupation to people in Canada is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It used to be done in "operations". I do not think it is continued now, but I would want to verify that before I give an answer.
Letters from overseas do not have a stamp.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: But my hon. friend's question related to censorship, whether the usual practice of letters being censored by the officer of the unit in which the man was serving was carried on. I do not think it is. I shall have to check. Perhaps some other member of the committee knows.

The reason I ask is that, in a letter I received to-day-naturally I will not divulge the source of it-it appeared that a soldier writing to his people at home indicated that it was impossible for him to write to his member of parliament, because, of course, the letter would be censored and, perhaps, would be destroyed. That was an experience which, he said, had happened to him before. I merely want to bring that to the attention of the minister because, if such things are going on, I think he ought to know about it and apply the necessary remedy, since certainly that sort of thing should not occur, particularly at this stage or, indeed, at any stage, with relation to letters of men in the ranks.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I quite agree. I think the nan to whom my hon. friend refers was probably under the impression that "operations" rules still applied and that letters were still aeing censored. Even under "operations" conditions, when letters were censored, there would be no justification or excuse for a letter being destroyed, or for the censoring officer refusing to send it forward unless it contained matter which was definitely contrary to public safety and so on.

I have a brief question to ask. I suppose I did not ask my question of the minister direct enough when I was getting some figures into the record to-night, but he has been in the habit of rising and replying to those who have put questions to him, and I should like the minister to reply to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The reason I did not do so is that my hon. friend has such a flair for figures that he rather inundated me at that time, and I thought perhaps I had better

carefully review to-morrow morning in Hansard what, he said and try to give him the reply a little later.
Thank you.

Is the British government setting a standard of food for our forces overseas? I know thoroughly well the difficulties of supplying the troops with food and equipment; they go through certain channels; but from what the minister said a few minutes ago the implication would be that, if the British government should decide to reduce the rations of our men, we would abide by their decision. Has the Canadian army a standard of food for our soldiers? If so, why are we not living up to it, and why are we being guided by what the Labour government of Great Britain at the present time may specify as adequate rations for our men? We should have a standard of food the same as the United States have, and live up to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can answer that question only by saying, as I did before, that we have served with the British troops; our ration standard has conformed to theirs; we use the same sources of supply; we draw our rations from their supply organization; and I for one feel that unless the British see fit to reduce their ration scale very much below what it now stands at, we should conform pretty much to that scale, whatever the Americans may see fit to do.

I should like to direct one or two questions to the minister. First, with regard to the Royal Military College at Kingston, would the minister inform the committee what the plans are, when it is proposed to open it, what the size will be, whether there will be one class or two classes, and will the numbers be 50, or 150, or 250?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I realize the interest my hon. friend has in this topic. I wish I could give him definite information to-night, but I cannot. My answer must be very much the same as I gave with regard to the future of the naval college at Royal Roads, that this whole matter of service colleges is now under review. Military training will be continued at the Royal Military College, but what the nature of' the instruction will be, and so on, is now being reviewed and considered, and an announcement will be made as soon as a decision is taken.

I have another question. I
hope the minister realizes the importance of this. Before the war there were perhaps fifty or sixty recruits coming in annually, and these were chosen more or less geographically across Canada. It is important that some

Demobilization-Army
announcement be made before the estimates come down. The question was asked on the order paper at the first of this month, do you intend to open the college with a class of 250 pupils; will it be one company or two companies? Whatever basis you decide upon, it will effect the boys in the collegiate institutes, the secondary schools and the private schools, and of course the parents of the boys themselves should be informed. No doubt the qualifications will be much the same as in the past, a certain academic standing, and selections made geographically. I would urge the minister as strongly as I can to make an announcement before the session closes, for this is a matter of importance. Could the minister tell us why the military college was closed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know.
Royal Roads was not closed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not know. I wa3
not minister at the time.

I am informed that there is
a difference of opinion. But the college should never have been closed: that is my opinion, and I say so to the committee. It was not closed in the last war.
The minister will recall that I directed a question on Monday September 10, just after the session opened, regarding boys who wanted to enter universities. The question I asked was, would the Minister of National Defence kindly inform the house , whether steps can be taken to speed up the discharge or release from the service of members of the armed forces whose applications for discharge have been made in order that they can attend or reenter universities or other educational institutions? The matter is urgent owing to shortness of time within which they can write to or correspond with a university.
I thank the minister for the cooperation he has given so far. If I am correctly informed, the house met here on a Thursday and I directed that question to the minister the following Monday. I believe it deals with something which is of interest to nearly every lion, member. Letters were received after Y-J day from the boys themselves and from their parents inquiring why they could not obtain their release from the army in order to attend university. Probably my question should have been directed to the Prime Minister, but as I said, I addressed it to the Minister of National Defence, and a good deal of publicity has been given to the matter. I have here a clipping which came to me from overseas, and I wish to correct the statement that "releases are going satisfactorily". I want to make it clear that
I appreciate the cooperative attitude of the Minister of National Defence, who is also the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, and I thank him and the officials of these departments who have made it possible for these boys to enter universities.
I think we should have a statement from the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Gibson) who is in the house at the moment, because in my opinion it is a shame and a disgrace to think that so many young men who entered the service at the age of eighteen and who are now twenty-three or twenty-four years of age are still in the service. I can cite dozens of instances. I must nave had communications with respect to at least fifty who are still in the service. I do not know whether there exists any feeling of prejudice between the different services, but, as anyone in the army knows when he is overseas, no one is indispensable. It is true that some of these young men may be _ doing clerical work, but when one considers the situation of a young man of twenty-three or twenty-four years of age; when one considers his anxiety to enter university, and then realizes that he has to wait another year, one will appreciate how these men must feel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that hundreds of members of the air force have got out for the very purpose of going to university, and I do not know why there should be any allegation that the air force is not cooperating in letting men out in order to go to university. Many hundreds of them are doing so.

Notwithstanding what the minister has said, I think he will bear me out that many of these boys have been kept in the service when they should have been let out. After all, no one is indispensable. I know that instructions were sent out, covering two mimeographed pages, informing those in the army and navy exactly what procedure had to be followed, but I do not believe it was done in the air force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: Yes; that was done by the air department,

If that is so, I am inclined to think that the men in charge of the stations resent instructions from headquarters. They no doubt say to themselves, "We are not going to be interfered with by headquarters", and the result is that these boys have been penalized. I know it is difficult to determine where the blame attaches. I do not know on whom the onus rests.
There is another matter in regard to which I should like to get some information, and that is, how these various units got their
Demobilization-Army

names. Take eastern Ontario units. In eastern Ontario we have the S.D. and G.'s, and men from these various units will be coming back to Canada. I should like to know how they got their names on going overseas.
How will they be unscrambled?
I am referring at the moment to the Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry regiment. How is it composed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot answer the question as to how these various regiments got their names. A good many of the regiments have a long tradition and a long association with the communities in which they were formed, and I must confess that I am unable to give their history. I do not know how they started and perhaps some officers who have had long experience can give that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend the member for York South knows all about this, but I may say that when the militia was reorganized in 1936 several changes were made in the names of regiments, in some cases causing a feeling of soreness, because old traditions had to be shattered in an effort to effect a composite militia force. We had in cooperation with us the defence association, the artillery association and the splendid body of militia men throughout Canada, and the resulting organization, which was completed about December 1936, commanded, I believe, the general commendation of all those who had served faithfully in the militia. In that transformation there were changes of names and thdre were new aggregations and formations.

I thank the acting leader of the house for the information, but it seems to me that every time anyone says anything in connection with this war some reference is bound to be made to the last war. In the last war we had the first, second and third battalions, in the first brigade and so on, and there was a second division. In my case we had the old second battalion from Ottawa and eastern Ontario. It was in the first brigade, the first division, and then came the twenty-first battalion, and the same all along the line. Some different idea, however, seems to have crept into this war. The idea seems to have been that everything should be different from what we had in the last war-no bands or anything of that sort, not even the bagpipes. I do not think the acting leader .of the house is quite right in what he has said. I am not putting any blame on the present minister, but in eastern Ontario, in
[Mr. Kidd.l
the last war, we had what was known as the second battalion, composed of every unit from Ottawa, Cornwall, Kingston, Brocbville, Belleville, Cobourg, Peterborough and so on. That battalion in this war was composed of the Hastings and Prince Edward infantry. Later on came the S.D.G.'s, comprising men from Cornwall, Brockville, Kingston and Peterborough. I do not know how this last unit obtained its name. I hope the minister will do everything he can to see that there is not a recurrence of this confusion. I hesitate to bring this matter up, because I do not wish to have it inferred at all that we are trying to bring any influence to bear upon officers and men, since no finer unit ever served overseas. When these boys come back they will go back to the various districts from which they were enlisted: Peterborough, Kingston, and so on.

There are one or two questions I wish the minister to answer in connection with the N.R.M.A. troops. On October 1 he brought down a return which showed, among other things, how many N.R.M.A. troops were in the army of occupation on the 1st of September, 1945. That return will be found at page 603 of Hansard. The number given there is 1,778 N.R.M.A. troops actually with the army of occupation. I have had word from overseas to the effect that some troops have been told that all N.R.M.A. men are to be taken out of the army of occupation. That may or may not be correct. Can the minister say whether it is?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is not correct.
It is not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
There is another question with regard to the N.R.M.A. overseas. The minister said to-night that on September 30 there were 10,693 N.R.M.A. troops overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: On strength overseas.

There have already come back 1,217. As the minister knows, there has been serious complaint about N.R.M.A. troops being sent back in the first division units, although these troops have not been fighting. The second division units are coming back and the third division and then the fifth and then the fourth. If the government policy remains as it was in the case of the first division there will be quite a large percentage of these N.R.M.A. troops coming back with these other divisions, despite the fact that they have not been in action, and I take it

Demobilization-Army
that the government has no intention of changing the policy. It is laid down in paragraph 23 on page 8 of this booklet, "After Victory," which says:
Points will be scored by those called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act, who have gone overseas for all of their service, whether G.S. or N.R.M.A.
Apparently no distinction is made between men who have been in action and men who have not. If I am wrong in stating what the government policy is, as announced by the minister, I wish he would correct me. I repeat, my understanding is that these N.R.M.A. men will come back with the other divisions, just as they have done in the first division, depending on what their point score is under the present system.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct. So far as overseas is concerned no distinction will be made between so-called N.R.M.A. men and others. They will come home on their point score the same as any othqr soldier overseas.

Of course we disagree with that policy, and we point out to the minister that we think it is very unfair and that it will cause great dissatisfaction. However, if the government is setting that policy the responsibility rests on the doorstep of the ministry.
Then, with regard to the N.R.M.A. troops in Canada, a return was brought down on October 1, 1945, and is to be found at page 586 of Hansard. This return showed that on August 15, 1945, there were 35,950 N.R.M.A. troops in Canada or in adjacent territories. In the two months that have expired since, that figure has been cut to 33,207.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is Canada only, not adjacent territories. That does not include N.R.M.A. men in Jamaica.
What is the comparable figure as of October 15?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to get that.
The minister does not have that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not have it here.
To-night the minister gave a figure of 33,207.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I say that does not include the ones in adjacent territories; it may. I shall have to verify that. The memorandum which was handed to me restricts that number to Canada.

I would point out to the committee that if that figure does include those in adjacent territories, then it means that 2,743 men have been discharged from N.R.M.A,
personnel. That number of NJTM.A. troops have been discharged in the two months. It may be government policy gradually to let all these N.R.M.A. troops out in Canada. We should like to know whether or not that is the policy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are not being discharged ahead of others, but there will be sopie, of course, who are bound' to go out on medical grounds and that sort of thing.
They are going out in Canada on the point system too, are they?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I suppose they are going out on the point system. But, of course, the points in Canada are not yet down low enough to-
A lot of them have fifty points.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; that is for repatriation. Perhaps this should be made clear at once. Because these men come back in units with a point score of fifty or fifty-five, it does not mean that they are eligible for discharge in Canada. The present point score-I am speaking from memory on this and am therefore subject to correction-on which a man can go out is certainly not below 110. It is being brought down gradually. I am inclined to think it is 120. The next move will be down to 110, in any event.
Perhaps the minister can bring us figures to-morrow showing the number of N.R.M.A. men who have been discharged in the two months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think I undertook earlier in the evening to do that.
And the reasons for discharge.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Whether that can be broken down to reasons, I do not know. I can give the gross figures as to discharges.

If it is awkward I will not press the question. The minister also said that on October 15 there were 9,575 N.R.M.A. troops in Canada out on extended leave, which in effect means they are back in civil life doing civil jobs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Farm leave. My hon.
friend is familiar with the type of leave which can be given.

That is 1,340 more than were out on the same sort of leave on August 15, as shown by the return to which I have just referred. The figure then was 8,235, so that it looks as though the N.R.M.A. men are being allowed to slip away.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Still a lot to slip.
Demobilization-Army
On April 6, the minister told me that there were 20,000 N.R.M.A, troops in Canada who were available for infantry reinforcements overseas. To-night he said that there are 15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I said, about 15,000. Subsequently to April 1 others were sent overseas.
There are still about 15,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right,

Who can go over to serve in the army of occupation. That means that, including the 15,000 and the 10,693 overseas, there are more than enough N.R.M.A. troops available to fill up the whole army of occupation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If they were of the right categories and types and trades and officers and so on. That is a tall order.
Well, apart from the officers and the N.C.O.'s.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Tradesmen's groups. That
15,000	figure represents the figure given me as suitable for infantry duty.

I do not suppose the minister would seriously contend that there are not enough N.R.M.A. troops available either overseas or in Canada to fill up the army of occupation and allow all the men who have been in action to come home.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would doubt it, yes._ In numbers, yes. But I would not think for one moment that you would be able to get the right categories.

It must be close to the number, considering that there are only 13,000 in the army of occupation who were not volunteers for that army. We should like to know what the government plans to do with those N.R.M.A. troops in Canada; whether they are not more ot less useless and costing the country a great deal of money. We should like to know from the government what the intention is with regard to those troops. Are they still to be allowed to sit here? Are they to be sent overseas, or what is the policy? I think the country is entitled to have that information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I gave that answer earlier this evening.
No; the minister did not say what he intended to do with the N.R.M.A. troops in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I said that was a matter of government policy which would be announced in due course.
That has been the $64 question for five years.
Perhaps the minister can tell us what the troops are doing now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are' performing a great many useful and necessary duties in the divisions in connection with demobilization. They are working in the demobilization depots. There are a great many services which have to be performed in this country, which if the N.R.M.A. men are not there to do it, we would have to have G.S. troops perform. Until we get the other 150,000 or 100,000 troops back from overseas and demobilized, there is still quite a little to be done in Canada. So far as possible those men are being utilized for that purpose. The alternative, of course, would be to discharge them and let them compete for jobs with men who are waiting overseas.
No; the alternative would be to send them over to the army of occupation, but that is not government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I answered that once before. My hon. friend and none of his supporters were making that suggestion before the election.
I suggested that in my speech months ago.
The minister is afraid to suggest it after the election.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not before the election.

The minister cannot make any statements like that about me because they are not true. I took that stand right through. I took that stand when I spoke in the house on April 6 of this year, that those N.R.M.A. troops should be used for the army of occupation. That has been my stand throughout. The trouble is that the government is afraid to do that.
That is the answer.

I should like to press the request of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the Silver Cross be granted to foster mothers. Let me give the minister an example. A child two years of age was legally adopted, with all the papers completed by the county judge. The child was reared, and at seventeen and half years of age desired to join the army. Before acceptance into the army, it was necessary that consent be given by the foster parents. This was granted. The boy was killed on active service. He had left a will under which all his possessions were to go to his foster mother. The foster mother, who had no other offspring, states

Demobilization-Army
that her will was in favour of this boy. She has been denied the Silver Cross, which I think is distinctly unfair. I could not be satisfied with an unfavourable decision by any departmental committee. I ask the minister to take this matter in hand personally, and if he does not feel justified in rendering a favourable decision, to take it to cabinet council for consideration.

Has any consideration heen , given by the government to making reciprocal agreements with the governments of the other dominions, so that if any of their men wished to settle in Canada we would give them some help, and similarly if any of our men settled in other dominions those governments could extend rehabilitation benefits to them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think consideration has been given any such proposal. Perhaps this more properly comes under the department of my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs, but I think we have restricted our consideration of rehabilitation benefits to those who have served in our own forces.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To supplement what my colleague has said, the question raised by my hon. friend is now receiving active consideration.

I dislike to pursue this matter, because I realize what a tender subject it must be for the minister and what a magnificent job he is doing in withholding from the committee, for purposes which must be very important to the government, the information we are trying to get in regard to the disposition of the N.R.M.A. troops. I wish to congratulate him on the magnificent job he has done so far. However, this afternoon we got these facts about the N.R.M.A. troops in Canada. In answer to a question of mine the minister said that he did consider them a potential source of recruits for the army of occupation; but he added very quickly, "But I am not saying they will be used as such." That was so much. Then I think in answer to the hon. member for Vancouver South a moment ago the minister said that some of them were being let out on their point scores.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, I did not say that. I doubt if any of them have point scores high enough to be let out.

I wondered about that. Perhaps the minister will say whether they will be let out on their point scores in Canada, in the same way that volunteer soldiers are let out. The minister also said that the disposition of N.R.M.A. troops was a matter
of government policy which would be announced in due course. We have had a fairly clear definition of government policy in Europe. The policy there is that no distinction is made between N.R.M.A. personnel and volunteers; and I think that is a very fine policy. But as another part of that policy, as I said this afternoon this government is prepared to conscript volunteers over there without hesitation. I suggest that the same thing could be done here. Five months have elapsed since V-E day, when it was realized that the N.R.M.A. troops in Canada would not be needed for actual fighting operations.
I do not think the minister can satisfy the committee any longer by simply saying that the disposition of these troops is a matter of government policy for the future. I would hazard the guess that the government policy for the future is decided now, but that it is inexpedient to announce it.
I would ask the government to tell us first of all, is it proposed to discharge N.R.M.A. troops in Canada on their point score? Second, when he said he considered them a potential source of recruits for. the army of occupation, was he giving his personal opinion or the opinion of the government? What did he mean by saying that they might not be used? Finally, how does he reconcile the existence of a conscripted force which we will not send for duty with the army of occupation, with the existence of a volunteer force which' he will conscript for such duty?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
So many questions are
wrapped up in what my hon. friend has said that I shall have to look at Hansard to-morrow to see if I can sift them out and answer them one by one. I made a pretty full statement on the position of the N.R.M.A. men, both at the session last April and here to-night. I would remind my hon. friend that the government has the responsibility for determining policy and will announce that policy in due course. When the government is decided on that policy, he will learn it. I do not want to give him any offence, but he cannot compel me or any member of the government to announce it to him before that time.

The minister said that certain N.R.M.A. troops were employed as operational troops. Would he tell us what those operational troops are? I am afraid I missed the actual number, because I could not hear it.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The number is 1,285. I am afraid I cannot answer the rest of my hon. friend's question, as to just what those troops are. I know some operational troops with
Demobilization-Army

N.R.M.A. men are in Jamaica, 'but I am rather under the impression that they are not included in those figures, for the reason I gave the hon. member for Vancouver South. However, I am going to check with my officials to clear that up to-morrow, and I will give my hon. friend the information as to what operational units in Canada now include N.R.M.A. personnel.
Can the minister tell us what courses are being carried on at the Royal Military College at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is closed at the moment.
There is a course going on, is there not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: As I understand it, I believe at present there are two wings of the staff course, the intermediate and junior wings, being carried on. I believe those are the two courses being given at the present time.
How many officers are attending?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to get that information, unless my parliamentary assistant can give it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe there are forty-eight in the intermediate wing, but I could not say about the other.
Could the minister say something about this Canadian army university course, as to whether these, boys have any hope of getting back?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am going to ask my parliamentary assistant to answer that question, since he is familiar with the details.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member for York South passed over to me some time agft a letter which I believe he had received from the father of one of these lads. I told him I would give him a report on the matter, but I am afraid I may have delayed in doing so.
I did ask for the report but did not follow it up, so that I cannot give him one in writing. However, the information I have is not quite in accord with what the hon. member said to-night. As I understand it, these courses were started in the fall of 1942 for the purpose of getting what could be termed good potential officer material in the army. The men were recruited from different high schools and colleges and offered the chance to enlist in the army and be given one year's tuition in the university, during which time they would follow what I suppose would be the equivalent of C.O.T.C. or basic training. Afterward they were sent to advanced training in the arm 
for which they had been found suitable. The first course did graduate in the fall of 1943. Everybody did go to the advanced training, eventually to the officers training centres and graduated as officers and were sent overseas as such.
The first course yvas considered such a success that the second one was started on a much more extensive scale. I understand that about 1,000 men were enlisted in the second * course, and were sent to numerous universities throughout the country. When the time came for them to be assessed1 as to the arm of the service in which they should be given a chance to qualify as officers, the spring of 1944 had arrived. Conditions overseas had changed considerably and, as hon. members know, casualties in the infantry were particularly high, compared with those in other arms of the service.
These young men, before going to advanced training, were told that they would not be needed as officers in the other arms of the service, and that if they did want to have an opportunity of going up and being assessed as potential officers they would have to go into the infantry, because that was where the need for officer reinforcements then existed. They were given the option at that time either of continuing their training as officers in the infantry, or to continue their training as other ranks, and1 to proceed in their own arms as other ranks overseas. In that connection they were asked to sign a waiver.
Would the parliamentary assistant read that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It reads:
To accelerate my training the undersigned soldier, graduate of No. 2 Canadian army university course hereby waives the privilege of appearing as officer candidate before the officer selection appraisal board in Canada.
When speaking earlier this evening, my hon. friend said that these men were made to sign a waiver. I do not believe he intended to say that any force had been used to 1 induce them to sign. I have made enquiries and I am informed that the men were definitely given a choice. They were told that they could keep on in their training as officers, but that they would not go to R.C.A. or engineers, as the case might be. It was pointed out that if they were going to be officers they would have to go to the infantry, because that is where the officers were needed. A considerable number of them agreed. They were further assessed to be officer material, were trained as infantry officers and went overseas as such. The others

Demobilization-Army
desired, rather than to do that, to go across as other ranks in their particular arms. They have done that.
There was a further step taken concerning which my hon. friend might like to have some information. In respect of these men who signed waivers on their privilege of appearing as officer candidates before the board -in Canada, in each instance C.M.H.Q. overseas was informed of the training received by these men. It was pointed out that such men had been considered as officer material in Canada, and it was suggested that particular attention be given to them in connection with the selection of officers overseas, if such took place.

I think that to a great extent the information given by the parliamentary assistant is correct. But many of these boys, when they went to university, were well under army age; and it was because they had accepted this training in the universities and because they had attended officers training corps, that they went on under the military corps to the various training centres to complete their training. The letter I read tonight. makes it appear that very few of them spent much time in England. The particular boy in question was in Italy within a few weeks of his arrival in England. I do not think there is much weight in the point made by the parliamentary assistant when he says that C.M.H.Q. were advised of the capabilities and training of these men, because I do not think they had enough time in England to go on with their training. They were trained men and, as such, they were shipped right into action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have no information as to the number of them who proceeded immediately to a theatre of war, or who were kept in the United Kingdom and are still there. If my hon. friend wishes to have that information, I shall endeavour to get it.

Would there not be ' some way in which those thousand boys who attended that course would get points for the time they were at university? It will be remembered that the reason those courses were started was that at the time they were started the R.C.A.F. had combed the country and was getting the best type of young men for that force. The then minister of national defence felt-and rightly so-that he must have a source of supply for good officer material in the future. With that in mind he went around to these public and private schools, got in touch with the most likely looking boys and practically pleaded with them to go to university for their training. There has been a great injustice done to those young
fellows. To a very great extent they began their military training when they were well under military age, and to-day they are being penalized.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If I might interject, it seems to me that the suggestion made is a very good one. They were enlisted at the time they went to university, so that I should think that would count for service in Canada.
Well, it is not being counted, and I think that would be a way to remedy it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We certainly will look into the matter and see what the answer is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not taken any part in the discussion on this particular matter, nor do I propose to do so to-night. However, I should like to leave on the record half a dozen questions the minister might answer to-morrow. I do not propose to debate them at this time. It is just a matter of ascertaining certain facts which no doubt he can provide.
Before proceeding to those questions, however, there are two matters to which I should like to refer. One has been discussed within the last few minutes. I do not know whether I understood the minister correctly-he will tell me, of course, if I did not-but I thought he said that certain N.R.M.A. personnel had been returned from overseas and were not being discharged, the reason being that their point score was not high enough; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is my information, yes.
I would like the minister to check up on that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then, low-point N.R.M.A. men have been returned from overseas and are being kept in uniform in Canada to-day. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; and so are other low-point men, who are not N.R.M.A. personnel.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I just wanted to know whether I had the correct understanding of it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The point I wish to make is that the point' system for repatriation, under the unit system, is not the same as the point system for discharge. A man with 50 points and up, provided that he is in the unit, would be entitled to be repatriated. However, speaking from memory, I believe the present point score which would entitle him to discharge is 120.
Demobilization-Army

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was surprised that N.R.M.A. men who were not qualified under the regulations for discharge should have been brought back, and not only that, but are si til being kept in Canada in uniform.
I have another question to ask which perhaps the minister cannot answer. I asked this perhaps three weeks ago when he made his first statement on some phase of these estimates. This whole appropriation of $3,365 million is made up of $2,000 million of interim supply from the session of this spring and $1,365 million which is now described as being for war expenditures and demobilization. I asked the minister if it would be possible to divide that large appropriation into three parts. The first would be a figure which might roughly include our commitments for war expenditures; that is, past commitments. Another would be the cost of demobilization as distinct from what one would ordinarily call war expenditures. The third would be for defence services of the future. It is possible the minister cannot give such a break-down. If he cannot, I do not press him to go to any bother to obtain it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
When my hon. friend asked these questions a week or two ago I discussed them with the officials of the department to see whether it would be possible to make the break-down. Of course everything is possible, but I felt at the time that it might be extremely difficult and that feeling was confirmed. Perhaps this is not the time to do it, but when we are discussing the figures I would be glad to give the reasons which have been given to me and which commend themselves to my judgment as being good reasons why it is not possible to break it down in the way my hon. friend has suggested.
The broad reason is that the whole thing is running along side by side. Take the item of pay and allowances, for' instance. It is almost impossible to allocate'what portion is for demobilization purposes just because we have to keep our troops on the other side on account of lack of shipping to bring them back. The same thing applies to equipment expenditures. In this case there is a carryover from the previous year and that sort of thing. When we come to consider the detailed estimates with regard to commitments for equipment and the like we have to consider commitments in the previous years which are a carryover into this year. I am told, and I believe it to be the case, that it would1 be extremely difficult to break it up into the heads my hon. friend has suggested.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not press the matter, because I realize it would be very difficult to do it. However, I think it would be valuable information to have had if it could be broken down in that way.
I have a dozen questions here to ask, three or four of which have arisen out of the discussion of the last half hour while others deals with other matters. I will ask them so that they will be on Hansard and can be answered b\r statements of fact which perhaps the minister will give when he continues these estimates to-morrow or later on.
First, what was the total number of men called up for service under the National Resources Mobilization Act, such statistics to be broken down by years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think I gave the total in my statement, and I will break it down by years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Some of these questions may have been partly answered before.
Next, what was the total cost of the N.R.M.A. army during each of the following fiscal years, 1941, 1942, 1943, 1944, 1945 and 1946 to date, these statistics to be broken down into the major items comprising the totals?
Next, do the cost figures include the cost of erecting training centres, barracks and other buildings for these men? If not, how much of the total cost of all such erections for all ' army purposes should properly be charged to N.R.MA. personnel? It may not be possible for the minister to make a clear cleavage.
If it is not, perhaps some fair estimate could be made.
Next, is it the intention of the government that the National Resources Mobilization Act shall remain on the statute books? These questions deal with some other casual matters. How many Canadian troops, if any, are serving at bases in the western hemisphere outside of Canada, for instance, in Labrador, Newfoundland and the British West Indies? Are any United States troops now serving in Canada?
If so, how many and where are they stationed?
Is it contemplated that a plan of cadet training for public and high school students will be carried out?
Have all Canadian prisoners of war been returned to Canada? If not, what is the reason for any delay? How many enemy prisoners of war are in Canada at present? How many have been returned to Germany or Italy? Are any arrangements likely to be

Judges Act-Ruling
made for securing payment from enemy countries for the cost of maintenance of these prisoners? I imagine I know what the answer to that last one will be.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think most of that information can be. readily obtained, although piobably not for to-morrow. I will get it as soon as I can and place it on the record, as my hon. friend has suggested.
Progress reported.

speechtext:

Wednesday, October 31, 1945.
